## 7.3 The hardware contract: what CLC promises

Before reading `clc_consume` you need the semantics the kernel leans on. Chapter 2.12 quotes the hardware contract in full (the ISA sentences on `try_cancel` and the response, both undefined-behaviour rules, the CUTLASS scheduling model, and W33/W34 verbatim); this subsection keeps only the points Sections 7.4-7.6 lean on directly, states each in one or two lines, and adds the ISA sentences Chapter 2 does not use (the `.cluster`-scope / generic-proxy sentence, the exit rule, the unspecified fourth element). Sources: PTX ISA 9.4 (docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/, 9.7.15.18 `clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel` and 9.7.15.19 `clusterlaunchcontrol.query_cancel`, read from the full ISA text), the CUDA Programming Guide section "Work Stealing with Cluster Launch Control" (docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.1.0/cuda-programming-guide/04-special-topics/cluster-launch-control.html, sections 4.12.1.1, 4.12.1.2, 4.12.2.2), the CUTLASS documentation page "Blackwell Cluster Launch Control" (docs.nvidia.com/cutlass/latest/media/docs/cpp/blackwell_cluster_launch_control.html) and the Colfax Research article "Dynamic persistent tile scheduling with Cluster Launch Control (CLC) on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs" (research.colfax-intl.com, fetched 2026-10-03). Where I quote, the words are the source's.

1. **What `try_cancel` does** (full quotation in Chapter 2.12.1). PTX ISA: "The clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel instruction requests atomically cancelling the launch of a cluster that has not started running yet. It asynchronously writes an opaque response to shared memory indicating whether the operation succeeded or failed. The completion of the asynchronous operation is tracked using the mbarrier completion mechanism at .cluster scope. This instruction accesses its mbarrier operand using generic-proxy." The grid is launched with one cluster per 256 x 256 output tile (32 x 32 = 1024 clusters, Chapter 3); only 33 of them can be resident (measured, note D.3); the other 991 sit in the hardware's launch queue and are what the resident clusters steal. The last ISA sentence matters for 7.4.4: the *mbarrier* side of `try_cancel` is generic-proxy, while the *response write* is async-proxy (item 3), so the slot, not the barrier, is the cross-proxy location.
2. **What the response contains.** PTX ISA: "On success, the opaque response contains the ctaid of the first CTA of the canceled cluster; no other successful response from other clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel operations from the same grid will contain that id." The second clause is the exactly-once guarantee the whole dynamic schedule rests on: the kernel never has to de-duplicate tiles.
3. **Multicast, completion, and the exit rule.** PTX ISA on `.multicast::cluster::all`: "the response is asynchronously written using weak async-proxy writes to the corresponding local shared memory addr of each CTA in the requesting cluster. The completion of the writes to addr of a particular CTA is signaled via a complete-tx operation to the mbarrier object on the shared memory of that CTA." Two consequences that shape Sections 5 and 7: (a) every CTA gets its own copy at the *same CTA-relative offset*, so every CTA can read its own slot without any cross-CTA traffic; (b) every CTA's *own* full barrier receives the 16 transaction bytes, so the full side of the pipeline is per-CTA while the producer is a single warp in rank 0. The next ISA sentence is an exit rule: "The behavior of instruction with .multicast::cluster::all qualifier is undefined if any CTA in the cluster is exited." No CTA may exit while rank 0's scheduler can still issue a multicast `try_cancel`; the kernel satisfies this because every role in every CTA consumes the final (not-cancelled) response before leaving its loop, and that response answers the last query the scheduler ever issues, so the last `try_cancel` precedes every exit in the cluster (7.6.8; note 7.10 gives the mbarrier-side reason).
4. **Size.** The response is 16 bytes (`.b128`); CUTLASS models it as `struct CLCResponse { uint32_t data[4] = {0}; };` with the comment "CLC response is an opaque 16B value" (cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:73-74), stored `alignas(16)` (`:95`); the kernel sets `transaction_bytes = CLCResponseSize = sizeof(CLCResponse)` (sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:155, :516). This is the 16 of `kClcTxBytes`.
5. **Decoding.** After the completion is observed, `clusterlaunchcontrol.query_cancel.is_canceled.pred.b128` yields the success predicate and `clusterlaunchcontrol.query_cancel.get_first_ctaid.v4.b32.b128` yields `{x, y, z, _}` of the cancelled cluster's first CTA. PTX ISA (9.7.15.19): "The contents of the 4th element are unspecified" (that is the `_` in W34's `{%0, %1, %2, _}`), and "If the request fails the behavior of clusterlaunchcontrol.query_cancel.get_first_ctaid is undefined." The Colfax article draws the practical rule: "if `.is_canceled` returns false then `query_cancel` instructions other than `.is_canceled` results in undefined behavior, so we should always start with `.is_canceled`."
6. **One requester per cluster.** The Colfax article: "with `try_cancel` only one thread per cluster should be used. In particular, multiple threads submitting `try_cancel` will result in multiple clusters being cancelled." The Programming Guide (4.12.1.1): "The preferred way to use Cluster Launch Control is from a single thread, i.e., one request at a time." and "Since thread block cancellation is a uniform instruction, it is recommended to submit it inside invoke_one thread selector." This is why the issue is under `elect_one_sync()` (W2) and why only rank 0 runs a scheduler (7.6.1, 7.6.6).
7. **No request after an observed failure.** PTX ISA: "If the executing CTA has already observed the completion of a clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel instruction as failed, then the behavior of issuing a subsequent clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel instruction is undefined." Programming Guide (4.12.1.2): "Submitting another cancellation request after observing a previously failed request is undefined behavior." This is why each scheduler iteration issues query t and then consumes response t (explicit.cu:847, then :853), and why the loop condition on response t decides whether iteration t + 1, and with it query t + 1, is ever entered: a query is never issued after a failure has been *observed*; at most one is in flight when the failure *occurs*, which the rule permits (7.6.7). Every other role loop exits on the same not-cancelled response.
8. **The first-CTA id is cluster-aligned.** Programming Guide (4.12.2.2, the cluster case): "The result received by all thread blocks corresponds to the local block index `{0, 0, 0}` within a cluster." With cluster (2,2,1) and a grid that is a multiple of the cluster in every dimension (`check_cluster_dims`, explicit.cu run(); `static_assert(kGridX % kClusterX == 0 && ...)` in util.hpp), the first CTA of any cluster has even `blockIdx.x` and even `blockIdx.y`. Measured: "every valid first-CTA id is even" (note D.3).

**The 16 bytes, as the compiler reads them (measured, not a contract).** Note D.2 decoded the SASS of `is_canceled`/`get_first_ctaid` as a bit-field extraction of the `LDS.128` result: `is_canceled` = bit 0 of word 2; `x0 = word0`, `y0 = word1 & 0xffff`, `z0 = word1 >> 16`. D.2 flags this layout as "inferred from the extraction code". The kernel does **not** rely on it: it only ever reads the response through the two `query_cancel` instructions (W34), exactly as CUTLASS does, so a future layout change would be absorbed by ptxas. Keep it that way when you write your own.

```
 response slot (16 B at smem_base + OFF_CLC_RESPONSE + 16 idx), as decoded by the SASS (note D.2, inferred):

   byte  0        4        8        12       16
         +--------+--------+--------+--------+
         | word0  | word1  | word2  | word3  |
         +--------+--------+--------+--------+
          x0        y0 (lo16) | z0 (hi16)   bit0 = is_canceled      (word3: not read)
```

---

## 7.4 Section 5: `clc_consume`, line by line

The banner and the function, verbatim:

```
///////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
// 5. [PROD] CLC LAYOUT  CLC consume (every participating warp, once per tile; Section 7.4, B.3.4 steps 5b-5c)
//   The scheduler warp of rank 0 asks the hardware for another cluster's work through clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel (section 7);
//   the 16-byte response is written into every CTA's clc_response[idx] (multicast::cluster::all) and completes every CTA's clc_full[idx].
//   Each participating warp (warp 2, rank-0 warp 1, warp 0, warps 4-7: 32 + 4 x (32 + 32 + 128) = 800 threads cluster-wide) then:
//     wait own full[idx] (parity phase); decode; fence.proxy.async; remote arrive on CTA 0's empty[idx] (count 800); ++state (2 slots);
//   and maps the cancelled cluster's first-CTA id (x0, y0), always even, to this CTA's tile:
//     (tm, tn) = (2 (y0 / 2) + x0 % 2 + x, 2 (x0 / 2) + y0 % 2 + y)     (swizzle_and_rasterize + AlongN transpose, B.4)
//   Example: response (x0, y0) = (10, 6) in CTA (x, y) = (1, 0) -> (tm, tn) = (7, 10): rows [896, 1024) of A, columns [1280, 1408) of D.
//   A not-cancelled response (valid == 0) ends the persistent loop of every warp; its x0/y0/z0 are stale and are not read.
//   Slots: response idx at OFF_CLC_RESPONSE + 16 idx (352, 368); full at 208 + 8 idx; empty at 224 + 8 idx (CTA 0's are the ones used).
//   TraceKind: 0 (no record), K_CLC_SCHED (rank-0 warp 1 lane 0), K_CLC_MMA (warp 0 lane 0); [TRACE] only.
///////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
template <uint32_t TraceKind>
__device__ __forceinline__ bool clc_consume(uint32_t smem_base, uint32_t x, uint32_t y, uint32_t& clc_idx, uint32_t& clc_phase,
                                            uint32_t& clc_count, int& tm_next, int& tn_next, uint32_t tile) {
  EXPLICIT_WAIT(smem_base + OFF_CLC_FULL + 8u * clc_idx, clc_phase, WAIT_CLC_FULL, tile, 0u);    // consumer_wait (own CTA's full barrier)
  uint32_t x0 = 0, y0 = 0, z0 = 0;
  uint32_t const valid = clc_decode(smem_base + OFF_CLC_RESPONSE + 16u * clc_idx, x0, y0, z0);
  fence_proxy_async_shared_cta();                                                                   // work_tile_info_from_clc_response (:433)
  mbar_arrive_remote(smem_base + OFF_CLC_EMPTY + 8u * clc_idx, 0u);                                 // consumer_release -> CTA 0 (sm100_pipeline.hpp:1132-1135)
#if defined(CUTLASS_DEABSTRACTION_TRACE)   // [TRACE]
  uint32_t const rec_idx = clc_idx, rec_phase = clc_phase, rec_count = clc_count;
#endif
  advance<kClcStages>(clc_idx, clc_phase);
  ++clc_count;
  (void)clc_count;
  if (valid) {
    tm_next = static_cast<int>(2u * (y0 >> 1) + (x0 & 1u) + x);   // swizzle_and_rasterize + possibly_transpose_work_tile (AlongN), B.4
    tn_next = static_cast<int>(2u * (x0 >> 1) + (y0 & 1u) + y);
  }
#if defined(CUTLASS_DEABSTRACTION_TRACE)   // [TRACE]
  if constexpr (TraceKind != 0u) {
    if ((threadIdx.x & 31u) == 0u) {
      TRACE_RECORD(TraceKind, TraceKind == K_CLC_SCHED ? 8192 : 16384, x0, y0, z0, valid, rec_idx, rec_phase, rec_count,
                   valid ? uint32_t(tm_next) : 0u, valid ? uint32_t(tn_next) : 0u, 0);
    }
  }
#else
  (void)TraceKind;
#endif
  return valid != 0u;
}
```
(explicit.cu:664-706)

It is the explicit form of CUTLASS's `fetch_next_work`:

```
    scheduler_pipeline.consumer_wait(scheduler_pipe_consumer_state);
    uint32_t smem_addr = cute::cast_smem_ptr_to_uint(&clc_response_ptr_[scheduler_pipe_consumer_state.index()]);
    auto work_tile = work_tile_info_from_clc_response(smem_addr);
```
```
    scheduler_pipeline.consumer_release(scheduler_pipe_consumer_state);

    work_tile = swizzle_and_rasterize(
      work_tile.M_idx, work_tile.N_idx, work_tile.L_idx, work_tile.is_valid(),
      block_id_in_cluster_.x, block_id_in_cluster_.y);
```
(cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:468-470 and :474-478; lines 471-473 between them are the trace probe added for the note)

### 7.4.1 The signature (explicit.cu:677-679)

- `template <uint32_t TraceKind>`: 0 in production. The parameter exists only so that the two traced call sites (scheduler warp, MMA warp) can emit differently tagged records (K5b vs K5c) from one function body; `if constexpr (TraceKind != 0u)` is inside the `#if` and the `#else` branch voids the parameter, so the production instantiation `clc_consume<0u>` and the two named-kind instantiations (which are also 0 in production, explicit.cu:238-239) are the same code.
- `smem_base`: the CTA's own 32-bit `shared::cta` base (E.6.1 address-space rule: every asm operand is `smem_base + OFF_*`).
- `x, y`: `%cluster_ctaid`, needed only for the mapping.
- `clc_idx, clc_phase, clc_count` by reference: the caller's CLC consumer state, advanced here.
- `tm_next, tn_next` by reference: written **only** under `valid`; the caller keeps the current tile in `tm, tn` and copies `tm_next, tn_next` over at the end of its loop body (explicit.cu:794, 854, 947, 1073). They must be initialised by the caller (`int tm_next = tm, tn_next = tn;` at :773, 828, 906, 1021) so that the unconditional copy after a not-cancelled response copies a defined (and dead) value rather than an indeterminate one (note E.6.4).
- `tile`: only for the trace's `EXPLICIT_WAIT` arguments; vanishes in production.
- Returns `valid != 0`: `true` = a tile was stolen (keep looping), `false` = the queue was empty (every role exits its loop).

### 7.4.2 Line 680: wait on the CTA's *own* `clc_full[idx]`

`EXPLICIT_WAIT(smem_base + OFF_CLC_FULL + 8u * clc_idx, clc_phase, ...)` is W6 on the address `smem_base + 208 + 8 idx` with parity `clc_phase`.

- Why **own**: item 3 of 7.3. The hardware completes the full barrier at the same offset in *every* CTA of the requesting cluster. Nothing has to be forwarded between CTAs on the full side; CTAs 1-3's full barriers are completed entirely by remote actions (rank 0's `arrive.expect_tx` plus the multicast bytes, note 7.4) and the consumer just waits locally.
- Why the barrier was initialised with count **1 (+16 tx)**: `producer_arv_count = 1` (sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:510) because exactly one thread arrives per CTA per query (lane i of rank-0 warp 1 arms CTA i through `mapa`, Section 7.6.5), and the transaction count is the 16 response bytes. The phase completes when the pending arrival count reaches zero **and** the tx-count reaches zero (PTX ISA, mbarrier section; the Programming Guide's "when the countdown reaches zero, the barrier is complete for the current phase" is the arrival half). So the phase cannot complete before both the arming arrival and the hardware's 16 bytes have happened, in either order.
- Why parity `clc_phase`: response n lives in slot n % 2 and completes phase n / 2 of `full[n % 2]`; the consumer state after n advances is `{n % 2, (n / 2) & 1}` (7.2.1).
- Which responses this CTA waits for: all of them, in order; a consumer warp that skips one would be one phase behind for the rest of the kernel and would eventually wait on a parity that never comes (deadlock) or read a slot early. Note E.6.4: "A role that skips one consume deadlocks CTA 0's empty barrier."

### 7.4.3 Lines 681-682: the decode (W34)

```
// W34 [CLC]  PersistentTileSchedulerSm100::work_tile_info_from_clc_response (sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:409-436); the fence follows in C++.
// For a not-cancelled response (valid == 0) the predicated get_first_ctaid leaves x0/y0/z0 unwritten (D.3): read them only under valid.
__device__ __forceinline__ uint32_t clc_decode(uint32_t result_addr, uint32_t& x0, uint32_t& y0, uint32_t& z0) {
  uint32_t valid = 0;
  asm volatile(
    "{\n"
    ".reg .pred p1;\n\t"
    ".reg .b128 clc_result;\n\t"
    "ld.shared.b128 clc_result, [%4];\n\t"
    "clusterlaunchcontrol.query_cancel.is_canceled.pred.b128 p1, clc_result;\n\t"
    "selp.u32 %3, 1, 0, p1;\n\t"
    "@p1 clusterlaunchcontrol.query_cancel.get_first_ctaid.v4.b32.b128 {%0, %1, %2, _}, clc_result;\n\t"
    "}\n"
    : "=r"(x0), "=r"(y0), "=r"(z0), "=r"(valid)
    : "r"(result_addr)
    : "memory"
  );
  return valid;
}
```
(explicit.cu:577-595; the asm string is `work_tile_info_from_clc_response`, cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:416-428)

- `ld.shared.b128 clc_result, [%4]` reads the 16-byte slot at `smem_base + 352 + 16 idx` into a 128-bit register. A `.b128` load needs a 16-byte-aligned address: CUTLASS declares the slots `alignas(16)` (sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:95) and the explicit kernel asserts `OFF_CLC_RESPONSE % 16 == 0` (explicit.cu:164); 352 = 22 x 16. It is a *generic-proxy* read of data that the *async proxy* wrote; the ordering that makes the data visible is the mbarrier: the complete-tx that finished the phase is what our `try_wait` observed, the same acquire pattern as reading a TMA-loaded stage after `full[s]` (Chapter 4).
- `is_canceled.pred.b128 p1` then `selp.u32 %3, 1, 0, p1`: `valid` becomes 1 or 0.
- `@p1 get_first_ctaid.v4.b32.b128 {%0, %1, %2, _}`: executed **only when cancelled** (item 5 of 7.3: decoding a failed response is undefined behaviour). The fourth component is discarded (`_`).
- The subtle part: the outputs are declared `"=r"` (write-only). For a not-cancelled response the predicated instruction does not write them, so what `x0, y0, z0` hold afterwards is whatever the allocated registers held before: the `= 0` initialisation at explicit.cu:681 does **not** survive the asm (an `"=r"` operand need not be the register that held the 0). Measured (note D.3): "In all 33 K5b and 132 K5c records with `valid = 0`, the raw M/N/L fields equal the *previous* response's decoded first-CTA id". This is precisely why line 691 guards the mapping with `if (valid)` and why the trace record writes `valid ? tm_next : 0`. The initialisation to 0 is hygiene (a defined value before the asm, no uninitialised-variable diagnostics), nothing more.
- Why no `elect`: every lane of the warp performs the load and decode. The result is warp-uniform (same slot), the load is a broadcast from shared memory, and CUTLASS does the same; keeping it per-lane avoids a shuffle to broadcast `valid`/`x0`/`y0` to the other 31 lanes, which all need them (the producer warp's lanes compute the TMA coordinates from `tm, tn`; the epilogue lanes compute store coordinates). In the *baseline's* SASS the MMA warp's decode keeps only the `valid` bit (note D.2, on the five `LDS.128` decodes: "in the MMA warp only the valid bit survives (`get_first_ctaid` eliminated as dead)"). The same elimination is expected in the explicit kernel, since `mma_role` voids `tm, tn` (explicit.cu:883), but note G.3 reports only the inventory (`is_canceled` 4 and `get_first_ctaid` 4 in PTX, 4 `LDS.128` in SASS) and makes no statement about it: expected, not reported; check with `cuobjdump -sass` around warp 0's `LDS.128` if you need the fact.

### 7.4.4 Line 683: `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta`

W15 `fence_proxy_async_shared_cta()` (explicit.cu:418-425, Chapter 6.4.3) is the single instruction `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta;` with a `"memory"` clobber; the asm is `cutlass::arch::fence_view_async_shared`, cutlass/arch/barrier.h:727-736.

CUTLASS issues it right after the decode asm:

```
      cutlass::arch::fence_view_async_shared();
```
(cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:430 in this tree; explicit.cu's comment and the note cite it as `:433`, which is the `#endif` three lines below. This is not a shift caused by the trace probes: `git diff -U0 cb424739` on this file shows 31 insertions and 0 deletions in three hunks, `-445,0 +446,6` (the K5a probe inside `advance_to_next_work`), `-464,0 +471,3` and `-469,0 +479,22`, so lines 1-445, including the fence at :430 and the `#endif` at :433, are unchanged from the pristine commit; the comment is simply three lines off.)

**The proxy reasoning.** PTX has two "proxies" through which shared memory can be accessed: the generic proxy (ordinary `ld`/`st`) and the async proxy (TMA, `tcgen05`, and CLC's response write, which the ISA calls "weak async-proxy writes", item 3 of 7.3). The ISA's rule (9.7.10.28.2, Async Proxy): "Accessing the same memory location across multiple proxies needs a cross-proxy fence. For the async proxy, fence.proxy.async should be used to synchronize memory between generic proxy and the async proxy." On the instruction itself (the `membar`/`fence` section): "membar.proxy and fence.proxy instructions establish an ordering between memory accesses that may happen through different proxies", and "Value .async of the .proxykind qualifier specifies that the memory ordering is established between the async proxy and the generic proxy. The memory ordering is limited only to operations performed on objects in the state space specified" (`.shared::cta` here). Our slot is accessed by both proxies in alternation:

```
   async proxy      generic proxy        async proxy
   try_cancel n  -> ld.shared.b128   ->  try_cancel n+2        (same slot: n % 2 == (n+2) % 2)
   (hw writes)      (800 threads read)   (hw overwrites)
```

The read-after-write edge (response n written, then read) is ordered by the mbarrier completion, as explained in 7.4.3. The **write-after-read** edge (our read, then the hardware's overwrite two queries later) is what the fence protects: the consuming thread orders its generic read before anything it does afterwards in the async proxy's view, then signals the producer through the release arrive on CTA 0's empty barrier; the producer's acquire on that barrier (its `wait own empty[idx]`) and its subsequent `try_cancel` therefore come after every consumer's read. The Colfax article explains the same line in CUTLASS as "guarding against the next iteration's `try_cancel` from overwriting the SMEM before the current iteration is able to finish reading from that location." Without the fence, the memory model would permit the generic read to be satisfied after the async-proxy overwrite even though the arrive came after the read in program order.

Cost: one `fence.proxy.async` per warp per tile (13 pairs of `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA; FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S` in the baseline SASS: 5 CLC decode sites + 8 epilogue subtiles, note D.2; 12 in the explicit kernel, note G.3, because it has 4 consume sites). At one per ~28 us it is invisible in the timing.

### 7.4.5 Line 684: the remote release on CTA 0's `clc_empty[idx]` (count 800)

W10 `mbar_arrive_remote(smem_addr, cta_id)` (explicit.cu:357-367, Chapter 6.3.6) is two instructions, `mapa.shared::cluster.u32 remAddr32, %0, %1;` then `mbarrier.arrive.shared::cluster.b64 _, [remAddr32];`, the `pred` branch of `ClusterBarrier::arrive(smem_ptr, cta_id, pred)`, cutlass/arch/barrier.h:486-499.

`mapa.shared::cluster.u32 remAddr32, addr, 0` translates this CTA's `shared::cta` address `smem_base + 224 + 8 idx` into the `shared::cluster` address of the same offset in CTA 0; the `mbarrier.arrive.shared::cluster` then arrives there. In CTA 0 itself `mapa(addr, 0)` is the identity. In SASS `mapa` is not an instruction: the rank is inserted into byte 3 of the address (`PRMT ..., 0x654`, note D.2), which is the compiler-visible form of the fact that the rank lives in address bits [24,32).

**Why CTA 0's barrier, and only CTA 0's.** CUTLASS's `consumer_release` for this pipeline is

```
  CUTLASS_DEVICE
  void consumer_release(uint32_t stage) {
    detail::pipeline_check_is_consumer(params_.role);
    empty_barrier_ptr_[stage].arrive(params_.producer_blockid);
  }
```
(cutlass/pipeline/sm100_pipeline.hpp:1131-1135)

with `clc_pipeline_params.producer_blockid = 0;` (sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:509). The producer (the scheduler warp) exists only in rank 0 and waits on *its own* empty barrier (7.6.5), so consumers in every CTA must send their release to rank 0. The empty barriers of ranks 1-3 are initialised with count 800 like everyone's (explicit.cu:1140 runs in every CTA) but are never arrived on or waited for (note 7.4: "their empty barriers are initialized but never used").

**Why 800.** CUTLASS computes

```
    clc_pipeline_params.producer_arv_count = 1;
    clc_pipeline_params.consumer_arv_count = NumSchedThreads + cluster_size *
                                                 (NumMainloopLoadThreads + NumEpilogueThreads + NumMMAThreads);
    if (is_epi_load_needed) {
      clc_pipeline_params.consumer_arv_count += cluster_size * NumEpilogueLoadThreads;
    }
```
(cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:510-515)

with `NumSchedThreads = NumMMAThreads = NumMainloopLoadThreads = NumEpilogueLoadThreads = 32` (one warp each, `:137-140`) and `NumEpilogueThreads = CollectiveEpilogue::ThreadCount = 128` (`:141`; four warps). For beta = 0, `is_epi_load_needed` is false, so

```
800 = 32 (rank-0 warp 1) + 4 CTAs x (32 (warp 2) + 128 (warps 4-7) + 32 (warp 0))
```

(the 928 variant with warp 3 is the beta != 0 build; the baseline chooses between them at run time with a `selp.b32 928, 800`, note D.2; the explicit kernel hard-codes 800 and asserts the formula at explicit.cu:192). Exactly who arrives, per response:

| Contributor | CTAs | Threads per CTA | Arrivals | Where in the code |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| scheduler warp (warp 1) | rank 0 only | 32 | 32 | explicit.cu:853 |
| producer warp (warp 2) | all four | 32 | 128 | explicit.cu:793 |
| MMA warp (warp 0), leader **and** peer | all four | 32 | 128 | explicit.cu:913 |
| epilogue warps 4-7 | all four | 128 | 512 | explicit.cu:1028 |
| **total** | | | **800** | |

**Why the empty count is a *thread* count (800) and not a warp count (25).** Logically one elected arrival per warp would suffice. The kernel uses every lane because: (1) CUTLASS's `consumer_release` (above) has no election, every lane of every consumer warp executes `mbarrier.arrive`, so the count must be `consumer_arv_count` *threads*, and the explicit kernel reproduces the source's protocol rather than inventing one; (2) an elected release would be correct only *after* every lane of the warp has finished reading the slot, so it would need a `__syncwarp()` (or a shuffle of a "done" flag) before the single arrive, adding an instruction and a convergence point to every consumer warp per tile, whereas in the all-lanes form each lane's own arrive follows its own read and fence in program order and needs neither; (3) it would change the PTX inventory the note checks against the baseline (`mapa` 8 sites and the `mbarrier.arrive.shared::cluster` sites, note G.3). The cost is 800 remote arrivals per tile per cluster, once per ~28 us: negligible.

Why the release happens *before* the mapping (lines 684 vs 691): the mapping is register arithmetic on values already extracted from the slot; the slot can be handed back as soon as the read and the fence are done, which is as early as possible. CUTLASS orders `consumer_release` before `swizzle_and_rasterize` for the same reason (sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:474-478).

### 7.4.6 Lines 686-690: state advance and the dead counter

`advance<kClcStages>(clc_idx, clc_phase)` moves to the other slot and flips the phase every second response (7.2.1). The `rec_*` copies on line 686 exist only so the trace record can report the state *as used* by this consume (before the advance); in production the line is compiled out. `++clc_count; (void)clc_count;` is the trace's `state.count`; in production it is dead code the compiler drops.

### 7.4.7 Lines 691-694: the mapping

Derived in Section 7.5. Note that it is guarded by `valid` (7.4.3) and that it uses the *consumer's own* `(x, y)`: the same response produces four different `(tm, tn)` in the four CTAs, one quadrant of the 256 x 256 cluster tile each.

---

## 7.5 From `(x0, y0)` to `(tm, tn)`: deriving the mapping from CUTLASS

### 7.5.1 The CUTLASS path

`fetch_next_work` passes the decoded ids to `swizzle_and_rasterize(M_idx = x0, N_idx = y0, L_idx = z0, valid, block_id_in_cluster_.x, block_id_in_cluster_.y)` (sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:476-478). Inside the function (`:726-845`, the name at :728), the first block is the swizzle:

```
    // Swizzling is enabled if the swizzle size is greater than 0
    if (params_.divmod_swizzle_size_.divisor > 0) {
```
(cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:741-742)

Our run has `max_swizzle_size = 0` -> divisor 0 (host guard `params.swizzle_divisor != 0` rejects anything else, explicit.cu run()), so the whole block is skipped and `cta_coord_m = x0`, `cta_coord_n = y0` unchanged. Then:

```
    // Since we swap the grid x and y modes if raster order is AlongN, swap the M and N tile offsets when
    // raster order is AlongN.
    auto [new_cta_coord_m, new_cta_coord_n] = possibly_transpose_work_tile(
      params_.raster_order_, cta_coord_m, cta_coord_n, params_.divmod_cluster_shape_m_, params_.divmod_cluster_shape_n_);

    new_cta_coord_m += cta_in_cluster_offset_m;
    new_cta_coord_n += cta_in_cluster_offset_n;
```
(cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:827-833)

with

```
  CUTLASS_DEVICE
  static cute::tuple<int32_t, int32_t>
  possibly_transpose_work_tile(RasterOrder raster_order, int32_t M_idx, int32_t N_idx, FastDivmod divmod_cluster_shape_m, FastDivmod divmod_cluster_shape_n) {
    if (raster_order == RasterOrder::AlongN) {
      int cluster_m, remainder_m, cluster_n, remainder_n;
      divmod_cluster_shape_m(cluster_m, remainder_m, M_idx);
      divmod_cluster_shape_n(cluster_n, remainder_n, N_idx);
      M_idx = cluster_n * divmod_cluster_shape_m.divisor + remainder_m;
      N_idx = cluster_m * divmod_cluster_shape_n.divisor + remainder_n;
    }
    return cute::make_tuple(M_idx, N_idx);
  }
```
(cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:697-708)

### 7.5.2 The derivation

Both cluster divisors are 2 (cluster (2,2,1); `cluster_divisors 2 2` measured, note D.1 D10). Substituting `M_idx = x0`, `N_idx = y0`:

```
cluster_m = x0 / 2,  remainder_m = x0 % 2
cluster_n = y0 / 2,  remainder_n = y0 % 2
M_idx' = cluster_n * 2 + remainder_m = 2 (y0 / 2) + x0 % 2
N_idx' = cluster_m * 2 + remainder_n = 2 (x0 / 2) + y0 % 2
tm = M_idx' + x,   tn = N_idx' + y          (cta_in_cluster_offset = block_id_in_cluster = (x, y))
```

which is exactly explicit.cu:692-693 with `>> 1` for `/ 2` and `& 1` for `% 2`. Because `x0` and `y0` are even (7.3 item 8), the remainders vanish and the mapping collapses to

```
(tm, tn) = (y0 + x, x0 + y)
```

the form the note uses throughout (note 7.4, B.4). The explicit kernel keeps the general form because it is the verbatim arithmetic of the source (two shifts and two masks per tile cost nothing), and because it stays correct should a non-cluster-aligned id ever arrive.

The **initial tile** is the same function with the launch coordinate and zero intra-cluster offsets:

```
  WorkTileInfo
  initial_work_tile_info(ClusterShape cluster_shape) {
    return swizzle_and_rasterize(blockIdx.x, blockIdx.y, blockIdx.z, /*valid=*/true, /*cluster_offset_m=*/0, /*cluster_offset_n=*/0);
  }
```
(cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:368-371)

so `tm = 2 (blockIdx.y / 2) + blockIdx.x % 2`, `tn = 2 (blockIdx.x / 2) + blockIdx.y % 2`:

```
  int tm = static_cast<int>(2u * (blockIdx.y >> 1) + (blockIdx.x & 1u));
  int tn = static_cast<int>(2u * (blockIdx.x >> 1) + (blockIdx.y & 1u));
```
(explicit.cu:1175-1176)

Here the offsets are zero because `blockIdx` already contains the CTA's position inside its cluster (`blockIdx.x % 2 == x`, `blockIdx.y % 2 == y`), whereas the CLC id is the *first* CTA's id and the offset must be added back.

### 7.5.3 Why there is a transpose at all

The raster order is chosen on the host by

```
    if (raster_order_option == RasterOrderOptions::Heuristic) {
      if (tiles_n > tiles_m) {
        return RasterOrder::AlongM;
      }
      else {
        return RasterOrder::AlongN;
      }
    }
```
(cutlass/gemm/kernel/tile_scheduler_params.h:337-344)

The arguments are *cluster*-tile counts, not CTA-tile counts: `PersistentTileSchedulerSm100Params::initialize` sets `problem_tiles_m_ = problem_blocks.x / cluster_shape.m()` and `problem_tiles_n_ = problem_blocks.y / cluster_shape.n()` (tile_scheduler_params.h:1920-1921), and `initialize_swizzle` calls `get_rasterization_order(problem_tiles_m_, problem_tiles_n_, raster_order_option)` (`:1881`), i.e. 64 / 2 = 32 against 64 / 2 = 32 here. With 32 == 32 the `else` branch gives **AlongN** (measured `raster_order AlongN`, note D.1 D10; the explicit kernel's host guard requires `raster_order == kRasterOrderAlongN`). A second guard follows at `:1882-1895`: because the AlongN transpose puts the M clusters on grid y, whose limit is 65535, `new_grid_y = problem_tiles_m_ * cluster_shape.n()` is checked against `(1 << 16) - 1` and the order reverts to AlongM if it would overflow; 32 x 2 = 64 does not trigger it (note 7.4: "the 65535 grid-Y guard not triggering"). The launch grid is then transposed:

```
    if (raster_order == RasterOrder::AlongN) {
      // Swap grid.x and grid.y for AlongN rasterization order, since the CLC scheduler
      // will schedule in AlongM order by default.
```
(cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:238-240)

The untransposed CTA grid comes from `get_tiled_cta_shape_mnl` (sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:628-630), which the kernel calls with `TileShape{} = (256, 128, 64)` (the MMA tile) and `AtomThrShapeMNK{} = (2, 1, 1)` (sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:389-393):

```
tiles  = ceil_div(problem, tile_shape)                                  -> (ceil_div(8192, 256), ceil_div(8192, 128)) = (32, 64)
ctas_m = round_nearest(tiles_m * size<0>(atom_thr_shape), cluster_m)    =  round_nearest(32 * 2, 2) = 64
ctas_n = round_nearest(tiles_n * size<1>(atom_thr_shape), cluster_n)    =  round_nearest(64 * 1, 2) = 64
```

The `x 2` on M and `x 1` on N are the `AtomThrShape`: one 2SM MMA atom spans two CTAs along M, so the 256-row MMA tile is two 128-row CTA tiles, whereas along N one CTA owns the whole 128 columns (note 7.4 states the same result: "ctas_m = round_up(ceil_div(8192, 256) * 2, 2) = 64, ctas_n = round_up(ceil_div(8192, 128), 2) = 64"). With these two formulas you can reproduce the grid for any other problem shape. After the swap `grid = (64, 64, 1)` with **grid.x indexing N and grid.y indexing M**. Measured (note D.3), the hardware hands out clusters approximately in launch-linear order, i.e. with `blockIdx.x` running fastest (933 of 991 ids at their sorted position, 25 adjacent swaps); this is an observation, not a documented guarantee, and the kernel must not depend on it (note D.7). By putting N on x, consecutive clusters sweep along N within one 256-row band of M, which is what "AlongN" means. The price is that every id, launch or CLC, arrives in (N-ish, M-ish) order and has to be transposed back into (tm, tn): that is `possibly_transpose_work_tile`.

### 7.5.4 The launch-linear cluster id, and how `(tm, tn)` relate to it

Define the cluster coordinate `(CX, CY) = (x0 / 2, y0 / 2)` and the launch-linear cluster id

```
L = CY * 32 + CX = (y0 / 2) * 32 + x0 / 2
```

(note D.3 uses this id; the kernel never computes it). The 32 is the number of clusters per grid row after the AlongN transpose, `gridDim.x / clusterDim.x = 64 / 2 = 32` (grid x indexes N), so L is the position of the cluster in the order the hardware launches clusters, x fastest, then y: the launch-linear id. The hardware walks L upward (approximately, and measured rather than guaranteed; 7.6.9). The cluster tile is `(m, n) = (L / 32, L % 32) = (CY, CX)` in 256 x 256 units, and the four CTAs' 128 x 128 tiles are

| rank r | (x, y) | tm | tn | rows of A / D | columns of B / D |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | (0, 0) | y0 = 2 CY | x0 = 2 CX | [256 CY, +128) | [256 CX, +128) |
| 1 | (1, 0) | y0 + 1 | x0 | [256 CY + 128, +128) | [256 CX, +128) |
| 2 | (0, 1) | y0 | x0 + 1 | [256 CY, +128) | [256 CX + 128, +128) |
| 3 | (1, 1) | y0 + 1 | x0 + 1 | [256 CY + 128, +128) | [256 CX + 128, +128) |

Read the table against Chapter 8's geometry: the MMA pair {2y, 2y + 1} = {0, 1} (y = 0) shares `tn = x0` and differs in `tm` by 1, which is why one `tcgen05.mma.cta_group::2` can compute 256 rows (both CTAs' A) x 128 columns (both CTAs' 64-column B halves of the same `tn`); ranks 0 and 2 (x = 0) share `tm`, which is why A is multicast across y with mask `0x5 << x`. So `tm % 2 == x` for every tile a CTA ever receives (explicit.cu:777 relies on it), and the two pairs differ in `tn` by exactly 1.

### 7.5.5 Worked examples

**Example 1 (the comment's, explicit.cu:672).** Response `(x0, y0) = (10, 6)` consumed in CTA `(x, y) = (1, 0)` (rank 1):

```
tm = 2 * (6 >> 1) + (10 & 1) + 1 = 2 * 3 + 0 + 1 = 7      -> A rows / D rows   [128 * 7, 128 * 8) = [896, 1024)
tn = 2 * (10 >> 1) + (6 & 1) + 0 = 2 * 5 + 0 + 0 = 10     -> D columns         [128 * 10, 128 * 11) = [1280, 1408)
L  = (6 / 2) * 32 + 10 / 2 = 3 * 32 + 5 = 101; cluster tile (m, n) = (3, 5)
```

The other three CTAs of the same cluster map the same response to rank 0: (6, 10), rank 2: (6, 11), rank 3: (7, 11): the four quadrants of rows [768, 1024) x columns [1280, 1536).

**Example 2.** Response `(x0, y0) = (62, 30)` consumed in CTA `(x, y) = (0, 1)` (rank 2):

```
tm = 2 * (30 >> 1) + (62 & 1) + 0 = 30 + 0 + 0 = 30       -> rows    [3840, 3968)
tn = 2 * (62 >> 1) + (30 & 1) + 1 = 62 + 0 + 1 = 63       -> columns [8064, 8192)   (the last 128 columns of D)
L  = 15 * 32 + 31 = 511; cluster tile (15, 31)
```

Check: `tm % 2 == 0 == x` and `tn = 63` is odd, as it must be for y = 1.

**Example 3 (initial tile; explicit.cu:1093 is the kernel banner comment that states it, :1175-1176 the code quoted in 7.5.2).** `blockIdx = (5, 2)`: `tm = 2 * (2 >> 1) + (5 & 1) = 2 + 1 = 3`, `tn = 2 * (5 >> 1) + (2 & 1) = 4 + 0 = 4`; this CTA is `(x, y) = (1, 0)`, rank 1, of the launch cluster `(CX, CY) = (2, 1)`, `L = 34`. Consistent with Example 1's pattern: rank 1 has odd `tm`, even `tn`.

**Coverage.** 1024 distinct values of L (32 x 32), each handed out exactly once by the hardware (7.3 item 2), each covering four distinct `(tm, tn)` in the four CTAs: 4096 CTA tiles = (8192 / 128)^2, exactly once. Measured: "the 1024 cluster tiles are covered exactly once" (note D.3; verified again for the explicit kernel, note G.1).

### 7.5.6 What the order means for data movement (my analysis, from the measured order)

Because L increases approximately in hand-out order and `L % 32` is the N coordinate, consecutive hand-outs share one 256-row band of A (4 MiB in fp16) and walk across the 32 column bands of B. Note D.3 measured that "the resident clusters work on two (834 of 991 hand-outs) or three (157) adjacent 256-row bands of A at any moment, never on one", so the A working set of the whole GPU is 8-12 MiB at any time and all of B streams through L2 once per band of A. Chapter 3 quantifies the resulting L2/HBM traffic; the dispatcher's only contribution is to preserve the hardware's order without depending on it.

---

## 7.6 Section 7: `scheduler_role`, line by line

The banner and the function, verbatim:

```
///////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
// 7. [PROD] CLC mbarrier  CLC scheduler: warp 1 of rank 0 (Section 7.4, B.3.4; kernel :681-724)
//   Once per tile (so that at most one query is outstanding per cluster, D.3):
//     1. throttle: wait throttle_full[i] (count 32 = the producer warp of rank 0 arrived at the start of its tile), release throttle_empty[i]
//     2. wait own clc_empty[idx] (count 800: every consumer of the previous response of this slot has arrived, section 5)
//     3. lanes 0..3 arm CTAs 0..3's clc_full[idx] with mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx(16 B) through mapa (the response is 16 bytes)
//     4. one elected lane issues clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel: the hardware answers into every CTA's clc_response[idx] and
//        completes the 16 transaction bytes on every CTA's clc_full[idx]
//     5. consume the previous response like every other warp (section 5); this warp's 32 arrivals are part of the 800
//   Tail: 2 test_wait/wait pairs on clc_empty so that both slots are released before the CTA exits. Warp 1 of ranks 1-3 does nothing.
///////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
__device__ __forceinline__ void scheduler_role(uint32_t smem_base, uint32_t x, uint32_t y, uint32_t lane, int tm, int tn) {
  griddep_wait();                                                                              // (kernel :688)
  uint32_t thc_idx = 0, thc_phase = 0;      // throttle consumer
  uint32_t clp_idx = 0, clp_phase = 1;      // CLC producer
  uint32_t clc_idx = 0, clc_phase = 0, clc_count = 0;   // CLC consumer (this warp consumes too: its 32 arrivals are part of the 800)
#if defined(CUTLASS_DEABSTRACTION_TRACE)   // [TRACE]
  uint32_t clp_count = 0;
#endif
  int tm_next = tm, tn_next = tn;
  uint32_t tile = 0;
  bool valid;
  do {
#if defined(CUTLASS_DEABSTRACTION_TRACE)   // [TRACE]
    heartbeat(tile, HB_TILE_START);
#endif
    // throttle consumer_wait + consumer_release (all 32 lanes; PipelineAsync, dst_blockid 0) (kernel :693-695)
    EXPLICIT_WAIT(smem_base + OFF_THROTTLE_FULL + 8u * thc_idx, thc_phase, WAIT_THROTTLE_FULL, tile, 0u);
    mbar_arrive_remote(smem_base + OFF_THROTTLE_EMPTY + 8u * thc_idx, 0u);
    advance<kThrottleStages>(thc_idx, thc_phase);
    // advance_to_next_work (sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:438-451): producer_acquire (sm100_pipeline.hpp:1095-1104) + elected try_cancel
    uint32_t const full_addr = smem_base + OFF_CLC_FULL + 8u * clp_idx;
    EXPLICIT_WAIT(smem_base + OFF_CLC_EMPTY + 8u * clp_idx, clp_phase, WAIT_CLC_EMPTY, tile, 0u);   // wait own empty[idx]
    mbar_arrive_expect_tx_remote_pred(full_addr, lane, lane < 4u ? 1u : 0u, kClcTxBytes);   // lanes 0..3 arm CTAs 0..3's full[idx] with 16 bytes
    if (elect_one_sync()) {
#if defined(CUTLASS_DEABSTRACTION_TRACE)   // [TRACE]
      TRACE_RECORD(K_CLC_ISSUE, 8192, clp_idx, clp_phase, clp_count, full_addr, blockIdx.x / 2, blockIdx.y / 2, 0, 0, 0, 0);   // K5a
#endif
      clc_try_cancel(smem_base + OFF_CLC_RESPONSE + 16u * clp_idx, full_addr);
    }
    advance<kClcStages>(clp_idx, clp_phase);
#if defined(CUTLASS_DEABSTRACTION_TRACE)   // [TRACE]
    ++clp_count;
#endif
    valid = clc_consume<K_CLC_SCHED_KIND>(smem_base, x, y, clc_idx, clc_phase, clc_count, tm_next, tn_next, tile);   // fetch_next_work (:702-706)
    tm = tm_next; tn = tn_next;
    ++tile;
  } while (valid);
  // CLC producer_tail (sm100_pipeline.hpp:1041-1050): test_wait, then the blocking wait only if not done (Section 7.10 tail 2)
  #pragma unroll
  for (int i = 0; i < kClcStages; ++i) {
    uint32_t const done = mbar_test_wait(smem_base + OFF_CLC_EMPTY + 8u * clp_idx, clp_phase, 1u);
    if (!done) { EXPLICIT_WAIT(smem_base + OFF_CLC_EMPTY + 8u * clp_idx, clp_phase, TAIL_CLC, tile, uint32_t(i)); }
#if defined(CUTLASS_DEABSTRACTION_TRACE)   // [TRACE]
    heartbeat(tile, HB_TAIL);
    trace_tail(TAIL_CLC, clp_idx, clp_phase, tile);
#endif
    advance<kClcStages>(clp_idx, clp_phase);
  }
}

### 7.6.1 Who runs it, and why only rank 0 (explicit.cu:1194-1196)

```
  else if (warp_idx == 1 && is_cta0) {

```
(explicit.cu:1194-1196; `is_cta0 = (rank == 0u)` at :1105, `lane = threadIdx.x & 31u` at :1102)

CUTLASS: `is_participant.sched = (warp_category == WarpCategory::Sched) && is_first_cta_in_cluster` with `is_first_cta_in_cluster = cta_rank_in_cluster == 0` (sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:426, :451). The reasons are the hardware's: one `try_cancel` per cluster, or you cancel several clusters (7.3 item 6); and since the response is multicast to all four CTAs and completes all four full barriers (7.3 item 3), the other three CTAs need no scheduler of their own: their warp 1 prefetches the A/B tensor maps in the prologue (explicit.cu:1113-1116) and then falls through the dispatch chain and exits (note 7.3 step 7). Rank 0 is just a convention (`producer_blockid = 0`); any fixed rank would do, as long as every consumer releases to the same one.

### 7.6.2 Line 821: `griddep_wait()`

`griddepcontrol.wait` (W35, explicit.cu:599) mirrors `cutlass::arch::wait_on_dependent_grids()` at kernel `:716` in this tree (`:688` in the numbering explicit.cu's comment uses). It belongs to programmatic dependent launch (Chapter 11): it blocks until all prerequisite grids have completed and their memory operations are visible. Only two warps execute it in this kernel: warp 2 (before its first TMA load touches A and B) and rank 0's warp 1 (here); `ACQBULK` x2 in the explicit SASS (note G.3). Why the scheduler warp needs it is not stated in the source; my hypothesis is that a cluster of a dependent grid must not start cancelling (stealing) its own grid's clusters, and thereby committing itself to more work, before the dependency it was launched under has resolved. Mark that reasoning as (hypothesis); the observable fact is that CUTLASS puts the wait there and the explicit kernel keeps it.

### 7.6.3 Lines 822-824: three pipeline states

| State | Role of this warp | Stages | Start | Advanced at | Partner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `thc_idx, thc_phase` | throttle **consumer** | 2 | {0, 0} | :838 | rank-0 warp 2 (producer, `thr_idx, thr_phase = {0, 1}` at explicit.cu:766) |
| `clp_idx, clp_phase` | CLC **producer** | 2 | {0, 1} | :849 | the 800 consumers (release) and the hardware (fill) |
| `clc_idx, clc_phase` | CLC **consumer** | 2 | {0, 0} | inside `clc_consume` (:688) | the same as every other consumer warp |

All three advance exactly once per loop iteration, so after tile t they all point at slot (t + 1) % 2 with the parities of 7.2.1. The scheduler is the only warp that is a producer *and* a consumer of the same pipeline, which is why it carries two CLC states; CUTLASS gives it `ThreadCategory::ProducerConsumer` (kernel :503-505).

The producer side is in `producer_role`, rank 0 only, at the very start of each tile, before any TMA of that tile:

```

      mbar_arrive_local(smem_base + OFF_THROTTLE_FULL + 8u * thr_idx);                        // all 32 lanes (count 32)

(explicit.cu:783-787)

- **Counts 32 / 32.** `producer_arv_count = NumMainloopLoadThreads` (32), `consumer_arv_count = NumSchedThreads` (32) (kernel :546-547): both sides arrive with all 32 lanes and no election. The explicit kernel initialises both with `kThrottleCount = 32` (explicit.cu:1159-1160, warp 3, as CUTLASS's `initializing_warp = 3`, kernel :549).
- **Why the consumer's release is the remote form to CTA 0, which is itself.** CUTLASS's `PipelineAsync::consumer_release` is `empty_barrier_ptr_[stage].arrive(params_.dst_blockid);` (cutlass/pipeline/sm90_pipeline.hpp:1236-1238) with `clc_throttle_pipeline_params.dst_blockid = 0` (kernel :548); `arrive(cta_id)` is the `mapa` + `mbarrier.arrive.shared::cluster` form (barrier.h:383-385 -> :486-499). On rank 0, `mapa(addr, 0)` is the identity, so this is a local arrive wearing cluster clothes. The explicit kernel reproduces the form (W10) so that the PTX inventory matches (`mapa` 8 sites, note G.3); nothing would break if it were a local arrive, but nothing is gained either.
- **Why the producer's acquire is a blocking wait with no peek.** `PipelineAsync::producer_acquire` has no `try` preceding it in the kernel (kernel :661 in this tree calls `producer_acquire` directly, then `producer_commit` at :662), and in practice it never blocks (below), so a peek would be wasted.
- **What the throttle expresses.** `throttle_full[i]` completes when rank 0's producer warp has *begun* tile i (phase i / 2); the scheduler cannot issue query i before that. `throttle_empty[i]` completes when the scheduler has consumed token i; the producer waits on it before producing token i + 2, which it never has to wait for because the scheduler consumes tokens within microseconds of their production (7.6.9). The throttle is CTA-local: both barriers live in rank 0 and only rank 0's warps touch them.

```
  CUTLASS_DEVICE
  void producer_acquire(uint32_t stage, uint32_t phase, ProducerToken barrier_token) {
    detail::pipeline_check_is_producer(params_.role);
    // 1. Wait for empty barrier to be ready
    // 2. Set the transaction bytes set to occur on the Full barrier for all blocks
    if (barrier_token == BarrierStatus::WaitAgain) {
      empty_barrier_ptr_[stage].wait(phase);
    }

    full_barrier_ptr_[stage].arrive_and_expect_tx(params_.transaction_bytes, lane_idx_, uint32_t(lane_idx_ < cluster_size_));
  }
```
(cutlass/pipeline/sm100_pipeline.hpp:1094-1104)

`advance_to_next_work` calls `clc_pipeline.producer_acquire(clc_pipe_producer_state)` with no token (sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:443), i.e. the `PipelineState` overload whose `barrier_token` defaults to `{BarrierStatus::WaitAgain}` (sm100_pipeline.hpp:1027), so the `if` above is always taken: the scheduler's empty-barrier wait is always the blocking form with no preceding peek. That is why the explicit kernel has a single `EXPLICIT_WAIT` at :841 and no `mbar_try_wait` anywhere in `scheduler_role`.

- **The wait on own `clc_empty[idx]`** (count 800) is the write-after-read guard for the slot: the 800 consumers of the response that previously occupied slot `idx` (query n - 2) have all read it and fenced (7.4.4). For queries 0 and 1 the parity is 1 on a fresh barrier and passes at once (7.2.1); the slots are empty by construction.
- **Arming.** W13:

```
__device__ __forceinline__ void mbar_arrive_expect_tx_remote_pred(uint32_t smem_addr, uint32_t cta_id, uint32_t pred, uint32_t transaction_bytes) {
  asm volatile(
    "{\n\t"
    ".reg .pred p;\n\t"
    ".reg .b32 remAddr32;\n\t"
    "setp.eq.u32 p, %2, 1;\n\t"
    "@p mapa.shared::cluster.u32  remAddr32, %0, %1;\n\t"
    "@p mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx.shared::cluster.b64  _, [remAddr32], %3;\n\t"
    "}"
    :
    : "r"(smem_addr), "r"(cta_id), "r"(pred), "r"(transaction_bytes)
    : "memory");
}
```
(explicit.cu:393-405; the asm is `ClusterTransactionBarrier::arrive_and_expect_tx(smem_ptr, bytes, cta_id, pred)`, cutlass/arch/barrier.h:606-620)

  Every one of the 32 lanes executes the asm; the predicate `p = (pred == 1)` is true only for `lane < 4`, and lane i maps `full_addr` to CTA i's `clc_full[idx]` and performs one `arrive.expect_tx` of 16 bytes there. Why 4: the cluster has 4 CTAs (`lane_idx_ < cluster_size_` in the source; the explicit kernel hard-codes `lane < 4u` because its cluster is fixed at (2,2,1)). Why one lane per CTA rather than one lane doing four arrivals: the predicated form costs the same (one predicated instruction per lane, issued once per warp), needs no loop, and in SASS is `@!P2 SYNCS.ARRIVE.TRANS64.RED RZ, [PRMT(lane)], R9` with `R9 = 0x10` (note D.2). Why 16: 7.3 item 4.
- **Why `arrive.expect_tx` (fused) rather than `expect_tx` then `arrive`.** The full barrier has arrival count 1, and that single arrival *is* this instruction. Because a phase completes only when both the pending-arrival count and the tx-count are zero, the phase cannot complete before the arming lane has arrived, whatever the relative timing of the hardware's 16 bytes: if the bytes land first the tx-count goes transiently negative (the PTX ISA gives tx-count a signed range, -(2^20 - 1) .. 2^20 - 1) and the phase still waits for the arrival; if the arrival comes first the tx-count sits at +16 until the bytes land. Either way the consumers can only pass their `try_wait` after both. The ranges are PTX ISA 9.4 Table 43 for `.layout::v0` (the default, and the only layout this kernel uses): expected arrival count 1 .. 2^20 - 1, pending arrival count 0 .. 2^20 - 1, tx-count -(2^20 - 1) .. 2^20 - 1; so `mbarrier.init` counts of 800 and 256 are legal and a 16-byte (or 49152-byte) expectation cannot overflow. The Programming Guide states the two-sided rule in its own words: "When a barrier uses a transaction count, it blocks threads at the wait operation until all the producer threads have performed an arrive and the sum of all the transaction counts reaches an expected value" (Asynchronous Barriers, 4.10.6). This is the same reason the mainloop producer uses `arrive.expect_tx` with 49152 (Chapter 8).

### 7.6.6 Lines 843-849: the elected `try_cancel` and the producer advance

W33 `clc_try_cancel(result_addr, mbarrier_addr)` (explicit.cu:568-575, Chapter 6.8.2 and 2.12.2) is the single instruction `clusterlaunchcontrol.try_cancel.async.shared::cta.mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes.multicast::cluster::all.b128 [%0], [%1];` with no `"memory"` clobber; the asm is `issue_clc_query`, cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:398-403.

- Operands: `result_addr = smem_base + 352 + 16 clp_idx` (this CTA's slot) and `mbarrier_addr = full_addr = smem_base + 208 + 8 clp_idx` (this CTA's full barrier), both `shared::cta` addresses of rank 0. With `.multicast::cluster::all` the hardware writes the same 16 bytes to offset 352 + 16 idx **in every CTA** and performs a complete-tx of 16 bytes on the barrier at offset 208 + 8 idx **in every CTA** (7.3 item 3). The addresses are rank-0 addresses, but the semantics are "the corresponding local address in each CTA", which works because all four CTAs have the identical shared-memory layout (same `SharedStorage`; measured bases differ only in bits 24-25, note D.1 D5).
- `.async`: the instruction returns immediately; the response arrives later (median 1408 ns after issue, note D.3).
- Why `elect_one_sync()`: one request per cluster (7.3 item 6). The CUDA Programming Guide (4.12.1.1) gives the reason a single-thread selector is the recommended form: "Since thread block cancellation is a uniform instruction, it is recommended to submit it inside invoke_one thread selector." The SASS confirms the "uniform": `UGETNEXTWORKID.BROADCAST [UR4], [UR5]` is an unpredicated uniform-datapath instruction that issues once per warp, so the `ELECT` is folded away (note D.2); the PTX-level election is still required for correctness portability, and it is the contract the kernel writes (note E.6.6).
- No `"memory"` clobber on W33: the asm has none in the source either (`:398-402`). It does not read or write anything the compiler can see; its effects arrive through the mbarrier, which every subsequent wait observes with its own `"memory"` clobber.
- `advance<kClcStages>(clp_idx, clp_phase)` (:849): the next query uses the other slot; every second query flips the parity the producer will wait for, in step with the consumers' releases.

### 7.6.7 Lines 853-856: consume your own response, then decide

```
    valid = clc_consume<K_CLC_SCHED_KIND>(smem_base, x, y, clc_idx, clc_phase, clc_count, tm_next, tn_next, tile);   // fetch_next_work (:702-706)
    tm = tm_next; tn = tn_next;
    ++tile;
  } while (valid);
```
(explicit.cu:853-856)

The scheduler warp is one of the 800 consumers (its 32 arrivals are counted in `NumSchedThreads`), so it runs the same `clc_consume` as everyone else, on the response to the query it has *just* issued (same iteration: issue n at :847, consume n at :853). This is where the warp blocks for the query latency: its `EXPLICIT_WAIT` on `clc_full[idx]` returns when the hardware's bytes have landed (7.6.9 gives the numbers). The warp does not use `tm, tn` for anything but keeps them so the trace can report the mapped tile; in production the copy on :854 is dead and vanishes.

The loop ends on the first not-cancelled response (`valid == 0`). That is also the last query the warp ever issues: issuing another after observing a failure is undefined (7.3 item 7). Note the order inside one iteration: *issue query t, then consume response t*. Query t + 1 is only issued in the next iteration, which is only entered if response t was a success, so the kernel never issues after observing a failure.

### 7.6.8 Lines 857-867: the producer tail

Quoted again from Chapter 4.8.2 because the state variables `clp_idx, clp_phase` and the query count T are defined in this chapter:

```
  // CLC producer_tail (sm100_pipeline.hpp:1041-1050): test_wait, then the blocking wait only if not done (Section 7.10 tail 2)
  #pragma unroll
  for (int i = 0; i < kClcStages; ++i) {
    uint32_t const done = mbar_test_wait(smem_base + OFF_CLC_EMPTY + 8u * clp_idx, clp_phase, 1u);
    if (!done) { EXPLICIT_WAIT(smem_base + OFF_CLC_EMPTY + 8u * clp_idx, clp_phase, TAIL_CLC, tile, uint32_t(i)); }
#if defined(CUTLASS_DEABSTRACTION_TRACE)   // [TRACE]
    heartbeat(tile, HB_TAIL);
    trace_tail(TAIL_CLC, clp_idx, clp_phase, tile);
#endif
    advance<kClcStages>(clp_idx, clp_phase);
  }
```
(explicit.cu:857-867)

Its source:

```
  // Prevents early exit of producer blocks in Cluster.
  // Does NOT reset transaction bytes.
  // This should be called once before kernel exits.
  CUTLASS_DEVICE
  void producer_tail(PipelineState state) {
    detail::pipeline_check_is_producer(params_.role);
    for (int count = 0; count < Stages; ++count) {
      bool done = empty_barrier_ptr_[state.index()].test_wait(state.phase());
      if (!done) {
        empty_barrier_ptr_[state.index()].wait(state.phase());
      }
      ++state;
    }
  }
```
(cutlass/pipeline/sm100_pipeline.hpp:1037-1050)

**What it waits for.** Let T be the number of queries issued = the number of tiles the cluster processed (one query per tile, 7.6.9; this is the note's symbol in its tail formulas and Chapter 8's `n_tiles`, not the TMEM base T of Chapters 9-10). The producer state after the loop is `{T % 2, 1 ^ ((T / 2) & 1)}`. Tail step i behaves as the acquire for a would-be query T + i, i.e. it waits for the 800 releases of response T + i - 2: step 0 for response T - 2 (the second-to-last, a cancelled one), step 1 for response T - 1 (the final, not-cancelled one). Note 7.10 states it in those words: "the 800 releases of the second-to-last response, then the 800 releases of the final response".

**The parities for the measured tile counts** (note 7.4; verified by the K_TAIL records of the explicit run, note G.1: "CLC `((T+i) % 2, 1 ^ (((T+i) / 2) & 1))`"):

| T | after loop `{clp_idx, clp_phase}` | step 0 waits | step 1 waits |
|---|---|---|---|
| 32 | {0, 1 ^ (16 & 1)} = {0, 1} | `empty[0]`, parity 1 | `empty[1]`, parity 1 |
| 31 | {1, 1 ^ (15 & 1)} = {1, 0} | `empty[1]`, parity 0 | `empty[0]`, parity 1 (the advance wrapped and flipped) |
| 19 | {1, 1 ^ (9 & 1)} = {1, 0} | `empty[1]`, parity 0 | `empty[0]`, parity 1 |

Check one: for T = 32, response 30 used slot 0 and its 800 releases completed phase 15 of `empty[0]` (phases are numbered by the responses that lived in the slot: 0, 2, 4, ..., 30 -> phase 15), parity 15 & 1 = 1. The lesson of note 7.2 applies: "all `Stages` waits use the same parity only when `N % Stages = 0`, so a single parity must not be applied to every barrier."

**Why the tail exists.** There is no cluster-wide barrier at kernel exit (note 7.10). The 800 releases of the last two responses are *remote* arrivals from warps of ranks 1-3 into rank 0's shared memory; if rank 0 exited first, those arrivals would target the shared memory of a CTA that no longer exists (note B.6: "a CTA must not exit while peers may still arrive on its barriers"). The tail keeps rank 0's scheduler warp alive until both slots' barriers have received every arrival; rank 0's other warps have their own tails (producer tail, accumulator tail, dealloc handshake) for the same reason. Why two steps: `Stages = 2`, one per slot. There is a second, ISA-level reason for the exit discipline as a whole (7.3 item 3): "The behavior of instruction with .multicast::cluster::all qualifier is undefined if any CTA in the cluster is exited." Ranks 1-3 must not exit while rank 0 can still issue a multicast `try_cancel`; they cannot, because every role in every CTA consumes the final response before leaving its loop, and that response answers the last query the scheduler ever issues (7.6.7), so the last `try_cancel` precedes every exit in the cluster.

**Why `test_wait` first.** `mbarrier.test_wait.parity` is a non-blocking probe with no suspend; if the phase has already completed (the common case: the final response was consumed by everyone within a few microseconds, while this warp was itself consuming), the blocking loop is skipped entirely. Functionally the blocking wait alone would be sufficient (it returns immediately on a completed phase); CUTLASS chose the probe-then-wait form for this pipeline (and only this one), and the explicit kernel mirrors it so that the two `test_wait.parity` sites of the baseline's PTX (note D.2) reappear in the explicit PTX (`mbarrier.test_wait.parity 2`, note G.3). The scheduler's two `EXIT` sites in SASS (code addresses, not timings) are `0x2f80`/`0x2fe0` in the baseline (note D.2) and `0x1e60`/`0x1ec0` in the explicit kernel (note G.3). No tail duration was measured; what G.1 reports is the ordering of the `K_TAIL` records: the CLC tail records follow the pipeline formula `((T+i) % 2, 1 ^ (((T+i) / 2) & 1))` for every cluster's T, and one step-0 record legitimately precedes its CTA's last K5c by 32 ns, because step 0 waits for the releases of response T - 2, not T - 1. The `1u` argument of `mbar_test_wait` is explained in 7.2.3.

### 7.6.9 Why one query per tile, why at most one outstanding, and what was measured

**One query per tile.** Every iteration of every role's loop consumes exactly one response, and the scheduler issues exactly one query per iteration. A cluster that processes T tiles (the launch tile plus T - 1 stolen ones) therefore issues exactly T queries: T - 1 answered "cancelled" and one answered "not cancelled" (note 7.4). Over the launch: 1024 queries, of which `N_native` fail, where `N_native` is the number of natively launched clusters. Measured: `N_native = 33` (= `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveClusters`), 991 cancelled + 33 not cancelled (note D.3, D9). 33 and not 148 / 4 = 37 because "a 2x2 cluster needs two whole TPCs in one GPC" and 8 leftover TPCs (16 SMs: 64, 65, 122-129, 142-147) cannot be paired (note D.3; the TPC explanation is inferred there).

**At most one outstanding.** Chain the dependencies of one cluster:

```
producer warp 2 (rank 0):   begin tile t  --throttle_full[t%2]-->  scheduler: query t  --hw-->  response t (= tile t+1 or "none")
                            ... 128 k-tiles of loads for tile t ...                         ^
                            consume response t  <------------------------------------------+
                            begin tile t+1  --throttle_full[(t+1)%2]-->  scheduler: query t+1
```

Query t + 1 needs the producer to have begun tile t + 1, which needs the producer to have consumed response t (the end of its iteration t), which needs response t to have arrived. So query t + 1 is never in flight while query t is: **at most one query outstanding per cluster**, and query t (which fetches tile t + 1) is issued only after the loader has begun tile t (note D.7). Measured: "Never more than one query was outstanding per cluster (0 violations in 1024 queries); at most 25 were outstanding GPU-wide at any instant" (note D.3), and "a query is actually in flight only about 4% of the time" (note D.7).

**Why the throttle exists (CUTLASS's comment and my analysis).** The source comment reads "Throttle CLC query to mitigate workload imbalance caused by skews among persistent workers" (kernel :720 in this tree). Without it, the scheduler's loop would be gated only by the CLC empty barriers (count 800), i.e. by the slowest consumer of the response two queries back. Those releases happen *during* tile n (warps 0 and 4-7 consume response n at the start of their tile n, warp 2 after tile n's loads; 7.8), so query n + 2, which needs only `clc_empty[n % 2]`, could be issued while tile n is still running: during tile n the scheduler could have issued queries n + 1 and n + 2, and at the end of tile n the cluster would know tiles n + 1 (from response n), n + 2 and n + 3, up to three stolen-but-unstarted tile ids against exactly one (tile n + 1) with the throttle, while a faster cluster that has run out of work finds the queue empty. At the end of the grid that is pure tail imbalance: the last tiles would sit in the shared-memory slots of busy clusters while other SMs idle. Tying each query to the producer's *start* of a tile means a cluster never owns more than the tile it is loading plus one claimed id, so the hand-out tracks actual progress. The measured spread of tiles per cluster (32 for 13 clusters, 31 for 19, 19 for the probe-slowed cluster (0,0), note D.3) is the throttle working: the slow cluster simply took fewer tiles.

**Measured dynamics (note D.3; all numbers are from the traced CUTLASS run, and the explicit kernel reproduced the same dynamics, note G.1):**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Query latency (issue by the elected lane to consumption by the same warp), 1024 queries | min 736 ns, p10 800, **median 1408**, p75 1472, p90 1536, p99 1792, max 2336 ns; bimodal by cluster placement (768-928 ns for 14 clusters, 1408-1504 ns for 19); the explicit kernel's own trace build measured a median of 1024 ns (note G.2), a probe-placement artefact irrelevant to the Release comparison |
| Not-cancelled responses | not slower: median 1376, max 1504 ns |
| Scheduler's gap from consuming response n to issuing query n + 1 (= the throttle wait) | 28.8-37.7 us, median 30.8 us, in the 32 unprobed clusters (cluster (0,0), slowed to 54.35 us per tile by its K3/K4 probes, is excluded) |
| Per-tile time (trace build) | median 31.90 us in the CUTLASS kernel's trace (35.46 us in the explicit kernel's trace, note G.2); Release build 0.889 ms / 32 tiles = 27.8 us per tile |
| Responses | 991 cancelled (ids 33..1023, each exactly once) + 33 not cancelled |
| Hand-out order | approximately increasing launch-linear id: 933 of 991 at their sorted position, 25 adjacent swaps, no id displaced by more than 4, with same-tick ties broken by ascending id (the 991 issue timestamps fall on 950 distinct 32 ns `%globaltimer` ticks; other tie orderings give 32-62 inversions); within each cluster strictly increasing |
| First hand-out | id 33, to cluster (0,0), consumed 1.28 us after the first query |
| MMA warp's consume relative to the scheduler's | K5c of rank 0 follows K5b by 96 ns median: the only measured datum on how long the MMA warp sits on `clc_full` |
| Outstanding queries | never more than 1 per cluster; at most 25 GPU-wide |

The latency is therefore completely hidden from the scheduler (it waits ~30 us for the throttle and ~1.4 us for the response). For the MMA warp the question is different, and it pays to separate the *warp* from the *tensor core*. The MMA warp consumes response t at the *start* of its tile t (explicit.cu:913 is the first statement of its loop body; Chapter 9), immediately after issuing k-tile 127 of tile t - 1. Its position in time is gated by `full[s]` (:923, the TMA data landing) and `acc_empty[st]` (:918), *not* by `empty[s]`: `tcgen05.mma` is asynchronous and its completion is observed only through `tcgen05.commit` (:942), so the warp's issue position can run ahead of tensor-core execution by up to the 8 stages the ring holds. It therefore reaches `clc_consume` roughly one TMA latency (~1 us) after the producer issued load 127 of tile t - 1, which is also about when the producer began tile t and query t was issued. How far ahead of completion the warp really runs was not measured; the one measured datum is D.3's "K5c of rank 0 follows K5b by 96 ns median": the MMA warp's consume completes 96 ns after the scheduler warp's, which is what you would see if the MMA warp were already waiting on `clc_full` when the response lands, on most tiles rather than occasionally (my reading of D.3). This is harmless for throughput: the tensor core still holds the already-issued MMAs of up to 8 k-tiles (8 x 217 ns = 1.74 us of work at 27.8 us / 128 per k-tile, issued before the warp blocked), so a tensor-core bubble can appear only when the response latency exceeds that queue, i.e. above ~1.7 us, which is beyond p90 (1536 ns) and near p99 (1792 ns) (my analysis). The epilogue warps consume at the start of their tile, after the MMAs of the previous tile have completed, i.e. later still; how often they wait was not measured.

**What the kernel must not assume.** The hand-out order is a property of this hardware and this run; "the kernel must not depend on the order, D.7" (note 7.4). Nor on `N_native = 33`: "the kernel must work for any number of native clusters and any hand-out order" (note D.7). The explicit kernel satisfies this by construction: it uses only `valid` and the mapping, never the order, never a tile count, never a second `try_cancel` after a failure.

Why the order is *approximately* increasing (hypothesis): the CLC unit pops the next unlaunched cluster from the grid's launch queue, which is in launch-linear order. The swaps are not a timestamp-resolution artefact: D.3 broke same-tick ties by ascending id, so a same-tick pair is never counted as an inversion, and found that every one of the 25 inversions is a query issued in a *strictly later* 32 ns tick that received a *lower* id than an earlier one, i.e. the CLC unit served two requests out of their issue order (hypothesis: arbitration between SMs or GPCs on the way to the unit). The count 25 holds only under that tie-breaking convention (other conventions give 32-62). None of this is relied upon.

---

## 7.7 One CLC round trip: the sequence

Participants: rank 0's producer warp (warp 2, throttle producer), rank 0's scheduler warp (warp 1), the CLC hardware, and the consumer warps of each CTA r = 0..3 (warp 0, warp 2, warps 4-7; plus warp 1 in rank 0). Response n uses slot `i = n % 2`; the parities are those of 7.2.1 with `k = n / 2`.

```
 rank-0 warp 2            rank-0 warp 1 (scheduler)              CLC hardware                 consumers, every CTA r (0..3)
 (throttle producer)                                                                            w0, w2, w4-7 (+ w1 of rank 0)
 ---------------------    ---------------------------------      ------------------           -------------------------------------
 begin tile n:
  wait  throttle_empty[i]
        (parity 1^(k&1))
  arrive throttle_full[i]
        x32 (local)   --------> wait throttle_full[i] (parity k&1)
                                 arrive throttle_empty[i] x32
                                   (mapa -> CTA 0 == self)
  issue 128 k-tiles of
  TMA for tile n ...             wait own clc_empty[i] (parity 1^(k&1))
                                   <== completed by the 800 releases of response n-2
                                 lanes 0..3: mapa(clc_full[i], lane)
                                   arrive.expect_tx 16  -------------------------------->  CTA r's clc_full[i]: pending arrivals 1 -> 0,
                                                                                            tx-count 0 -> +16
                                 elected lane:
                                   try_cancel [resp[i]], [clc_full[i]] --> pop next unlaunched
                                                                           cluster (first CTA
                                                                           (x0,y0,z0)) or decline
                                                                           | 16 B async-proxy write to resp[i] of CTA 0,1,2,3
                                                                           | complete_tx 16 on clc_full[i] of CTA 0,1,2,3
                                                                           v                tx-count +16 -> 0  => phase k completes
                                 advance clp state
                                 consume (same code as ->)                                  each warp: wait own clc_full[i] (parity k&1)
                                   wait own clc_full[i]                                       ld.shared.b128 resp[i]
                                   decode, fence.proxy.async                                  is_canceled -> valid; @valid get_first_ctaid
                                   arrive CTA 0's clc_empty[i] x32 ----+                      fence.proxy.async.shared::cta
                                   advance clc state                   |                      arrive CTA 0's clc_empty[i] (x32 per warp,
                                   if valid: (tm,tn) <- (x0,y0)        |                        x128 for w4-7)  --------------------+
                                                                       |                      advance clc state                       |
                                                                       |                      if valid: (tm_next,tn_next) <- (x0,y0) |
  ... last TMA of tile n                                               v                                                              v
  consume response n  (w2 of rank 0 is one of the consumers)       CTA 0's clc_empty[i]: 800 arrivals -> phase k completes
  tm,tn <- tm_next,tn_next                                          (this is what the scheduler's acquire for query n+2 waits for)
 begin tile n+1  ------------->  (next iteration: query n+1)
```

Arrival bookkeeping on the figure: each CTA r contributes w0 (32) + w2 (32) + w4-7 (128) = 192 arrivals to CTA 0's `clc_empty[i]`; rank 0 adds its w1 (32), so rank 0 contributes 224 and the total is 224 + 3 x 192 = 800 (7.4.5).

Timing scale (measured, note D.3): the left column's "begin tile n -> begin tile n + 1" is ~28-32 us; the scheduler's query-to-consume is ~1.4 us; the MMA warp reaches its consume of response n at the start of its tile n, as soon as it has *issued* tile n - 1's last k-tile (about one TMA latency after the producer issued that load, i.e. about when query n was issued), typically before the response has landed, and then blocks on `clc_full[i]` while the tensor core drains the up-to-8 queued k-tiles (measured: its consume follows the scheduler's by 96 ns median, 7.6.9); the epilogue warps reach theirs at the start of their tile n, later still.

The slot and parity bookkeeping of the same round trips, for a cluster that processes T = 32 tiles:

| tile t | query / response n | slot | sched acquire: `empty[slot]` parity | consumers: `full[slot]` parity | gives |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 (fresh) | 0 | tile 1 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 (fresh) | 0 | tile 2 |
| 2 | 2 | 0 | 0 (releases of resp. 0) | 1 | tile 3 |
| ... | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... |
| 30 | 30 | 0 | 0 | 1 | tile 31 |
| 31 | 31 | 1 | 0 | 1 | "not cancelled": exit |
| tail 0 | (32) | 0 | 1 (releases of resp. 30) | | |
| tail 1 | (33) | 1 | 1 (releases of resp. 31) | | |
