## 7.8 Design notes: why the dispatcher has this shape, and how to reuse it

**Dynamic (CLC) instead of a static persistent stride.** A static persistent kernel would launch `N_native` clusters and have cluster c take tiles c, c + N_native, ...; but `N_native` is not known reliably in advance (33 here, not the arithmetic 37), and clusters do not run at equal speed (the probed cluster did 19 tiles). CLC lets the hardware be the queue: residency and speed differences are absorbed automatically, exactly-once coverage is guaranteed by the ISA (7.3 item 2), and the kernel needs no atomic counter in global memory. The cost is one 16-byte round trip per tile (1.4 us hidden behind 28 us) and, per CTA, 8 mbarriers (`clc_full[2]`, `clc_empty[2]`, `throttle_full[2]`, `throttle_empty[2]`: 8 x 8 B = 64 B at bytes 208..239 and 304..335) plus 2 x 16 B = 32 B of response slots (bytes 352..383): 96 B per CTA, 384 B cluster-wide, of which only rank 0's throttle barriers and `clc_empty` barriers are ever used (explicit.cu:109-110, 144-145, 148-149, 151).

**Two slots, not one or eight.** With the throttle guaranteeing at most one query outstanding, two slots are the minimum that lets query n + 1 be issued while the slowest consumers of response n (the epilogue warps, which consume at the start of their tile n) are still to read it; one slot would force the scheduler to wait for all 800 releases of response n before issuing n + 1, serialising the round trip with the slowest warp's tile boundary. More than two buys nothing because the throttle never lets a third be in flight. Where the 2 comes from: `kClcStages` mirrors `SchedulerPipelineStageCount`, a template parameter of the dispatch policy, not a hardware constant. The collective builder sets `SchedulerPipelineStageCount = cute::conditional_return<IsGroupGemm || IsRCGroupGemm>(8, 2)` (cutlass/gemm/collective/builders/sm100_umma_builder.inl:282), i.e. 2 for this dense GEMM, and passes it into `MainloopSm100TmaUmmaWarpSpecialized<Stages, SchedulerPipelineStageCount, AccumulatorPipelineStageCount, ClusterShape>` (`:320-322`; the measured instantiations are `MainloopSm100TmaUmmaWarpSpecialized<8,2,4,(2,2,1),Sm100>` and `PersistentTileSchedulerSm100<(2,2,1),2>`, note D.1); the kernel reads it back as `DispatchPolicy::Schedule::SchedulerPipelineStageCount` (sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:118) and sizes `CLCPipeline`, `CLCThrottlePipeline` and `clc_response[]` with it (`:172`, `:175`, `:200`). The CUTLASS documentation page says generically "The CLC pipeline has a depth of 3 to overlap the CLC operations of multiple waves for latency hiding"; that sentence describes a different configuration and does not apply to this build.

**The asymmetry of the barriers.** Full barriers are per-CTA and completed locally (by the hardware's multicast complete-tx plus a remote arming arrive), empty barriers are used only in CTA 0 (because the producer is one warp in rank 0). Both follow directly from the hardware contract and the single-requester rule; do not "symmetrise" them. In particular, do not make CTAs 1-3 wait on their own empty barriers (nobody arrives there) and do not make consumers arrive locally (the producer would never see them).

**Where each role consumes (Chapters 8-10 give the loops).** Warp 2 consumes response t *after* issuing tile t's loads, because it needs tile t's coordinates before the first TMA and only learns tile t + 1 from response t. Warps 0 and 4-7 consume response t *before* computing/storing tile t; the MMA warp needs no coordinates at all (`(void)tm; (void)tn;`, explicit.cu:883) and the epilogue needs the *current* tile's coordinates, which it already has. Consuming early releases the slot early. In all roles the fetched tile becomes current only at the end of the loop body, so the last tile is computed and stored *after* the not-cancelled response has been consumed (note 7.4).

**Failure modes to design against (each was a bring-up hazard, note E.6.4, E.6.7):**

| Mistake | Symptom |
|---|---|
| A role skips one `clc_consume` (e.g. an early `continue`) | CTA 0's `clc_empty` never reaches 800: the scheduler's acquire two queries later deadlocks the whole cluster |
| Producer parity started at 0 | the scheduler blocks forever on query 0 (a fresh barrier never completes its phase with nobody arriving) |
| Same parity for both tail steps | one tail step may pass early or hang depending on T % 2 (7.6.8) |
| Reading `x0/y0` when `valid == 0` | stale ids of the previous response (measured, D.3): a tile computed twice |
| A second `try_cancel` after observing a failure | undefined behaviour per the Programming Guide |
| Dropping the `fence.proxy.async` | a legal reordering lets the next response overwrite a slot a slow consumer has not read yet |
| A separate `mbarrier.arrive` issued *before* `expect_tx` | the arrival drops the pending count 1 -> 0 while the tx-count is still 0, so the phase completes immediately (ISA 9.7.15.16.8: completion when both counts are zero), before any response bytes exist, and the 800 consumers read a slot the hardware has not written yet; `expect_tx` then `arrive` would be safe, and the fused `arrive.expect_tx` removes the ordering question and matches the source |

**Generalising to other kernels.** The dispatcher is operator-agnostic: it hands out `(x0, y0, z0)` of a cancelled cluster and lets `swizzle_and_rasterize` turn it into work coordinates. To reuse it: (1) keep one scheduler warp in rank 0 and the fused arm-then-issue sequence; (2) set the full count to 1 + 16 tx and the empty count to the exact number of consumer *threads* cluster-wide (every warp that loops over tiles must consume every response); (3) arm `lane < cluster_size` CTAs; (4) keep the throttle unless your producer has a different natural "begun a tile" point; (5) replace the mapping with your own raster (for L > 1, bind `z0` to the batch coordinate as CUTLASS does: the baseline binds `word1 >> 16` to `L_idx`, note D.2; the explicit kernel drops it because L = 1 is fixed); (6) for a swizzled raster, implement the full `swizzle_and_rasterize` block (sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:742-826), which the fixed run skips; (7) for stream-K-style schedulers, honour `increment_pipe` (not every `fetch_next_work` consumes a response).

## Checkpoint

**1. A fresh mbarrier has just been initialised with count 800. Warp A waits on it with parity 1, warp B with parity 0. What happens to each, and which of the kernel's states (`clp_phase = 1`, `clc_phase = 0`) does each correspond to?**

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Warp A returns immediately: parity 1 names the "immediately preceding phase" of a barrier whose current phase has parity 0, and that preceding phase counts as complete (PTX ISA, mbarrier.try_wait; Programming Guide: a freshly initialised barrier has parity 0). Warp B blocks until 800 arrivals complete phase 0. A is the producer convention (`clp_idx, clp_phase = 0, 1`, explicit.cu:823): the scheduler must be able to use both empty slots before anyone has released them. B is the consumer convention (`clc_idx, clc_phase = 0, 0`, :824): nobody may read a response before it has landed.
</details>

**2. Derive the 800 of `kClcEmptyCount`. Which thread of which CTA is *not* counted, although it is alive during the mainloop?**

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
800 = NumSchedThreads + cluster_size x (NumMainloopLoadThreads + NumEpilogueThreads + NumMMAThreads) = 32 + 4 x (32 + 128 + 32) (sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:510-512; explicit.cu:183, asserted at :192). Contributors per response: rank 0's warp 1 (32), and in each of the four CTAs warp 2 (32), warp 0 (32, leader and peer alike) and warps 4-7 (128). Not counted: warp 1 of ranks 1-3 and warp 3 of every CTA, which exit after the prologue (and the beta != 0 build would add warp 3's 4 x 32 for 928). Every counted warp must consume every response or CTA 0's barrier never completes.
</details>

**3. Response `(x0, y0) = (18, 44)` is consumed in rank 3. Give `(tm, tn)`, the rows of A and columns of D this CTA will work on, and the launch-linear cluster id.**

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Rank 3 is `(x, y) = (1, 1)`. `tm = 2 (44 >> 1) + (18 & 1) + 1 = 44 + 0 + 1 = 45`; `tn = 2 (18 >> 1) + (44 & 1) + 1 = 18 + 0 + 1 = 19`. Rows [128 x 45, 128 x 46) = [5760, 5888) of A and D; columns [128 x 19, 128 x 20) = [2432, 2560) of D. `L = (44 / 2) x 32 + 18 / 2 = 22 x 32 + 9 = 713`; cluster tile (22, 9). Sanity: `tm % 2 = 1 = x`, and the pair partner rank 2 has `(44, 19)`, same `tn`.
</details>

**4. Why does `clc_consume` execute `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta` *after* reading the response rather than before, and which hazard would be exposed without it?**

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
The read-after-write direction (hardware wrote the slot, we read it) is already ordered by the mbarrier: the complete-tx that finished the phase is what our `try_wait` observed. The hazard is write-after-read across proxies: the same slot is overwritten two queries later by another `try_cancel` (async proxy). The fence orders this thread's generic-proxy read before its subsequent async-proxy-visible effects, the release arrive on CTA 0's `clc_empty` carries that order to the scheduler, whose acquire on that barrier precedes the next `try_cancel`. Without the fence the memory model allows the overwrite to be observed by the earlier read. (CUTLASS: sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:430 in this tree, cited as `:433` by explicit.cu's comment; the Colfax article gives the same reason.)
</details>

**5. The scheduler arms the full barriers with `arrive.expect_tx` *before* issuing `try_cancel`. Would the protocol still be correct if the hardware's 16 bytes could land before the arming arrival? Why?**

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Yes. The full barrier has arrival count 1 and the arming instruction is that one arrival fused with the expect. A phase completes only when the pending-arrival count and the tx-count are both zero, so until the arming lane arrives the phase cannot complete regardless of the tx-count (which may be transiently negative if the bytes land first; the PTX ISA gives tx-count a signed range). In program order the arming precedes the issue anyway (explicit.cu:842 before :847), so the question is moot for this kernel, but the fused form is what makes the mainloop's 49152-byte expectation safe too.
</details>

**6. A cluster processed T = 31 tiles. List the (barrier, parity) pairs of its two CLC tail waits and say which response's releases each one waits for.**

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
After 31 producer advances the state is `{31 % 2, 1 ^ ((31 >> 1) & 1)} = {1, 0}`. Step 0: `clc_empty[1]`, parity 0: the 800 releases of response 29 (the second-to-last, cancelled). Advance: wrap to index 0, phase flips to 1. Step 1: `clc_empty[0]`, parity 1: the 800 releases of response 30 (the final, not-cancelled one). Both barriers are CTA 0's. The tail keeps rank 0 alive until the remote arrivals from ranks 1-3 have landed (note 7.10).
</details>

**7. Explain, with the dependency chain, why the kernel never has two CLC queries outstanding in one cluster, and quote the measured scheduler-side waiting times that show the query latency is hidden.**

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Query t + 1 requires `throttle_full[(t+1)%2]`, which rank 0's producer warp arrives on only when it begins tile t + 1; it begins tile t + 1 only after consuming response t at the end of its iteration t; response t exists only after query t completed. So query t + 1 is never issued while query t is in flight (at most one outstanding, measured 0 violations in 1024 queries). The scheduler spends 28.8-37.7 us (median 30.8) per tile waiting for the throttle and about 1.4 us (median 1408 ns, max 2336 ns) waiting for the response (note D.3), so the round trip is hidden inside the ~28 us tile.
</details>

**8. What exactly does the production build see of `EXPLICIT_WAIT(addr, parity, WAIT_CLC_FULL, tile, 0u)`, and how do you prove from the artefacts that the trace helpers are absent?**

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
With the toggle off the macro is `#define EXPLICIT_WAIT(addr, parity, site, tile, q) mbar_wait((addr), (parity))` (explicit.cu:237): the call becomes W6, `mbarrier.try_wait.parity ... [addr], parity, 0x989680` in a `bra` loop; `WAIT_CLC_FULL`, `tile` and `q` are discarded by the preprocessor. Proof of absence: every helper is inside `#if defined(CUTLASS_DEABSTRACTION_TRACE)` (:618-662), the production PTX contains no `trap` (note G.3's absence list) and no `%globaltimer`, and two toggle-off builds give byte-identical SASS (note G.3, D6).
</details>

# Chapter 8. The Feeder: producer_role and load_ktiles (Warp 2)

**What you will learn**

- What the one producer warp of every CTA does for each of the 128 k-tiles of a tile: wait for a free ring slot, register 49152 expected bytes on the pair leader's `full[s]`, issue one multicast TMA load of A and one plain TMA load of B, and peek the next slot — and why every one of those four steps has exactly the operands it has.
- How a 128 x 64 A stage is assembled in every CTA out of two 64-row halves loaded by two different CTAs (the multicast across `y`), why B is split across the pair instead of multicast, and how six 8192-byte boxes add up to `2 x (16384 + 8192) = 49152` bytes on each pair leader's barrier while the peer's `full[]` barriers stay untouched for the whole kernel.
- Why `tm % 2 == x` for every tile a CTA ever receives (from the launch mapping and from the CLC mapping), and therefore why `a_row = 128 tm + 64 y` and `b_col = 128 tn + 64 x` are the right coordinates.
- The three bookkeeping details that make the producer semantics-identical to CUTLASS's `CollectiveMma::load`: the peek-before-wait token protocol (130 peeks per tile for 128 waits), the two rolled loops of 8 and 120 iterations, and the CLC consume placed after the loads instead of before them.
- The exit tail: eight blocking waits whose parity is 1 for any tile count, what the measured `K_TAIL` records say, and why a CTA that skipped them could free shared memory its pair leader is still reading.
- What the TMA unit does to the bytes it writes (`SWIZZLE_128B` = `Swizzle<3,4,3>`), why the stage bases must be 1024-byte aligned, why the k-tile is 64 wide, and why no line of this kernel ever computes a swizzled address.
- Why this warp's loop can be 37 SASS instructions long without costing a cycle of GEMM time.

Notation (from Chapter 1): rank `r = x + 2y`, pair leader = even rank, peer = `r ^ 1`, CTA 0 = rank 0, tile `(tm, tn)` in 128 x 128 CTA-tile units, k-tile `q` (0..127), stage `s` (0..7), `smem_base = 0x400 + (r << 24)` (measured, note D.1 D5), `OFF_*` as in explicit.cu. Chapter 6 explains the PTX of W6, W7, W12, W21, W22 and W35 character by character; Chapter 4 explains parities and tokens in general; Chapter 7 explains `clc_consume` and the scheduler warp; Chapter 9 the consumer side (`mma_role`). This chapter is about who calls those wrappers, on which addresses, with which numbers, and why.

---

## 8.1 Warp 2 in one picture

The producer warp is the only warp that moves A and B. It never reads a byte of them: it hands coordinates to the TMA unit, which writes the bytes into the 8-stage shared-memory ring (and, for A, into a sibling CTA's ring as well), and it manages the ring with two mbarrier arrays. Everything downstream (UMMA, TMEM, epilogue) is somebody else's job.

```
 global A (fp16, K-major)            global B (fp16, K-major)
 rows 128 tm + 64 y .. +64           columns 128 tn + 64 x .. +64
 k = 64 q .. +64                     k = 64 q .. +64
        |                                   |
        | W21: cp.async.bulk.tensor.3d      | W22: cp.async.bulk.tensor.3d
        |      .cta_group::2 .multicast     |      .cta_group::2 (no multicast)
        |      mask 0x5 << x                |
        v                                   v
 +-------------------------------------------------------------+
 | this CTA's smem ring, stage s (and, for A, the ring of the  |
 | sibling CTA that shares tm)                                 |
 |   OFF_SMEM_A + 16384 s + 8192 y  <- 8192 B of A (my half)   |
 |   OFF_SMEM_B +  8192 s           <- 8192 B of B (my half)   |
 +-------------------------------------------------------------+
        |  complete_tx: every box credits the PAIR LEADER's full[s]
        v
 full[s] of the pair leader: count 1 (+49152 tx)   --->  warp 0 of the leader (Chapter 9)
 empty[s] of every CTA:      count 2                <---  tcgen05.commit, mask 0xF, from both leaders
```

Per CTA and per tile the warp issues 256 TMA instructions (2 per k-tile), performs 130 non-blocking peeks and at most 128 blocking waits on `empty[]`, and — on pair leaders only — 128 `mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx` of 49152 bytes. The same warp also takes part in the CLC protocol once per tile (Chapter 7), and on CTA 0 it drives the throttle that bounds the scheduler.

---

## 8.2 The section banner (explicit.cu:708-722), step by step

```
///////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
// 6. [PROD] TMA mbarrier  Mainloop producer: warp 2 of every CTA (Section 7.5, B.3.1; CollectiveMma::load, sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:589-629)
//   Per k-tile q of the current tile (tm, tn), stage s = the producer's ring index (0..7, wraps; phase flips at each wrap):
//     1. wait empty[s] (parity prod_phase; count 2 = the two pair leaders' tcgen05.commit of the previous use of stage s)
//     2. leader lane of the pair leader only: mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx on its own full[s] with 49152 bytes
//     3. one elected lane issues two 2SM TMA loads, both completing on the PAIR LEADER's full[s] ((smem_base + 8 s) & ~(1 << 24)):
//        A  multicast to ranks x and x+2 (mask 0x5 << x), coordinates (64 q, 128 tm + 64 y, 0), destination OFF_SMEM_A + 16384 s + 8192 y
//           in both destination CTAs: this CTA supplies its 64-row half of the 128 x 64 A stage, the other cluster row supplies the other half
//        B  no multicast, coordinates (64 q, 128 tn + 64 x, 0), destination OFF_SMEM_B + 8192 s (this CTA's 64 N-columns)
//     4. advance {s, phase}; peek the next empty[] so that the blocking wait is skipped when the ring is free
//   Example: tile (tm, tn) = (5, 9), q = 7, rank 1 (x = 1, y = 0): A box (448, 640, 0) -> 0x01024800 (rank 1) and 0x03024800 (rank 3),
//   B box (448, 1216, 0) -> 0x01036800; rank 2 (x = 0, y = 1) writes its A half at 0x02026800 / 0x00026800 (offset + 8192).
//   Byte accounting per stage and pair: 2 CTAs x (2 A halves x 8192 + B 8192) = 49152 = the expect_tx of step 2.
//   After the last tile: 8 blocking waits (the tail) so that no stage is still being read when the CTA exits.
///////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
```

The header line names the role (warp 2 of every CTA — unlike the scheduler, which runs only on rank 0, and the MMA issue, which runs only on pair leaders), the hardware families it touches (`TMA`, `mbarrier`), and the CUTLASS function it mirrors: `CollectiveMma::load` in `include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:589-629` (verified: the function starts at line 589, `producer_try_acquire` at 604, `CUTLASS_PRAGMA_NO_UNROLL` at 607, the two copies at 620-621).

The four numbered steps are the body of one iteration of the k-tile loop:

1. **Wait `empty[s]`.** `empty[s]` is at `smem_base + OFF_MAIN_EMPTY + 8 s` = `smem_base + 64 + 8 s` (explicit.cu:140). Its arrival count is 2 (explicit.cu:182, `kMainEmptyCount = 2`) because the producer's next write to slot `s` overwrites two things that two *different* readers are using: (a) this CTA's own A stage and B half, which its **own pair leader's** `tcgen05.mma.cta_group::2` reads directly out of this CTA's shared memory (note B.6; the B half written at explicit.cu:754 has no other reader), and (b) through the A multicast (explicit.cu:747), the copy of this CTA's A half that sits in the sibling CTA `r ^ 2`, which the **other pair's leader** reads. Both leaders must therefore have finished their previous use of slot `s` before it may be refilled: count 2. CUTLASS computes the same number generically as `cluster_m / atom_m + cluster_n / atom_n - 1 = 2/2 + 2/1 - 1 = 2` (`include/cutlass/pipeline/sm100_pipeline.hpp:565-566`): the first term counts the MMA atoms along M that read this CTA's B (in CUTLASS's general form B is multicast along M; here one 2SM atom spans the cluster's whole M extent, so the term is 1 — the own leader), the second counts the atoms along N that read this CTA's A (A is multicast along N: 2 — the own leader and the other pair's leader), and the `- 1` removes the own leader, which both terms counted [the formula is from source; this reading of its terms is my analysis]. Each leader's release is a `tcgen05.commit ... multicast::cluster` with mask `0xF` (Chapter 9), so every CTA's `empty[s]` receives exactly two arrivals per use. The parity the producer waits for is its own `prod_phase`, which starts at 1 (Section 8.3).
2. **`arrive.expect_tx` 49152 on the leader's own `full[s]`.** Only the leader lane of a pair-leader CTA does this, once per k-tile. Section 8.4.4 derives the number and the "only".
3. **Two TMA issues by one elected lane.** The A load is multicast to the two CTAs with the same `x` (`0x5 << x` = ranks `x` and `x + 2`); the B load is not multicast. Both name the pair leader's `full[s]` as their completion barrier through the peer-bit trick `(smem_base + 8 s) & ~(1 << 24)` (Section 8.4.6).
4. **Advance and peek.** The state moves to the next slot and a non-blocking `try_wait` on that slot's `empty[]` produces the token that step 1 of the next iteration consumes (Section 8.4.5).

The example line is recomputed in Section 8.7.1 (it is correct), the byte accounting is derived in Section 8.5.3, and the tail in Section 8.6.8.
