## 8.3 ProducerState (explicit.cu:723-726)

```
struct ProducerState {
  uint32_t prod_idx = 0, prod_phase = 1;   // mainloop producer state (8 stages), carried across tiles
  int q = 0;                                // k-tile index inside the current tile
};
```

Three integers, and each initial value is forced:

- `prod_idx = 0`: the ring is used from slot 0; the consumer (warp 0, Chapter 9) also starts at slot 0, and both advance in lockstep through the same sequence of slots, so the n-th k-tile of the kernel lives in slot `n % 8` for both.
- `prod_phase = 1`: a freshly initialised mbarrier is in phase 0, and `mbarrier.try_wait.parity` with parity 1 asks "has the phase of parity 1 — the *preceding* phase — completed?", which is true at once (explicit.cu:607-609 states this; the CUTLASS origin is `make_producer_start_state`, `include/cutlass/pipeline/sm90_pipeline.hpp:254-260`, "Producer starts with an opposite phase as the buffers are initially empty"). The first pass over the eight `empty[]` barriers therefore never blocks: an empty ring is free by definition. Had the producer started at phase 0 it would wait for a release that never comes — a deadlock at `q = 0`, the symptom of the first row of the note's failure-mode table (E.7.2). That row lists the byte count, the arming lane, the barrier operand and the A mask as its causes; a wrong start phase is not among them but produces the same symptom. The start states themselves are fixed by note E.6.5 ("producers start `{0, 1}`, consumers `{0, 0}` (`make_producer_start_state`, `sm90_pipeline.hpp:254-260`)").
- `q = 0`: reset at the start of every tile (explicit.cu:779); it is in the struct, not a local of `load_ktiles`, because a tile's 128 k-tiles are issued by *two* calls (8 then 120, Section 8.6.5) and the second call must continue the k coordinate where the first stopped.

`prod_idx`/`prod_phase` are **carried across tiles and never reset**: the ring does not know about tiles. For this run every tile has 128 k-tiles and `128 % 16 == 0` (16 = two passes of the 8-slot ring flip the phase twice), so coincidentally every tile starts at `{0, 1}`; the code must not — and does not — rely on it (note E.6.5). `advance<kStages>` (explicit.cu:610-613) is the whole state machine:

```
template <uint32_t Stages>
__device__ __forceinline__ void advance(uint32_t& idx, uint32_t& phase) {
  if (++idx == Stages) { idx = 0; phase ^= 1; }
}
```

[derived from source] For the n-th k-tile counted from kernel start (`n = 128 t + q`), the producer uses slot `n % 8` and waits parity `1 ^ ((n / 8) & 1)`. Inside one tile: `q = 0..7` parity 1, `q = 8..15` parity 0, `q = 16..23` parity 1, ..., `q = 120..127` parity 0 (because `120 >> 3 = 15` is odd). Keep this table in mind for the tail (Section 8.6.8).

---

## 8.4 load_ktiles (explicit.cu:728-760), line by line

```
// One load() call: n k-tiles starting at state.q. Two calls per tile (8 then k_tiles - 8) give two rolled loops.
__device__ __forceinline__ void load_ktiles(ExplicitGemmParams const& params, ProducerState& st, int n, uint32_t smem_base,
                                            uint32_t a_dst_base, uint32_t b_dst_base, uint32_t full_masked_base, uint32_t empty_base,
                                            uint16_t a_mcast_mask, bool is_leader_lane, int a_row, int b_col, uint32_t tile) {
  uint32_t tok = mbar_try_wait(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);            // producer_try_acquire before the loop (:604)
  #pragma unroll 1                                                                          // CUTLASS_PRAGMA_NO_UNROLL (:607)
  while (n > 0) {
    if (!tok) { EXPLICIT_WAIT(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase, WAIT_MAINLOOP_EMPTY, tile, uint32_t(st.q)); }   // producer_acquire (sm90_pipeline.hpp:531-536)
    if (is_leader_lane) { mbar_arrive_expect_tx_local(smem_base + OFF_MAIN_FULL + 8u * st.prod_idx, kMainloopTxBytes); }   // (:537-539), leader lane, 49152
    uint32_t const s = st.prod_idx;                                                          // write_stage
    advance<kStages>(st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);
    tok = mbar_try_wait(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);                     // peek the next stage, unconditional (:617)
    if (elect_one_sync()) {                                                                  // one election for the A+B pair (:619-622)
      int32_t const c0 = 64 * st.q;
#if defined(CUTLASS_DEABSTRACTION_TRACE)   // [TRACE]
      if (TRACE_IN_FIRST_CLUSTER()) {   // K4a: coordinates, destination, elements, unmasked local full[s] (C.4.3)
        TRACE_RECORD(K_TMA_LOAD, 128, uint32_t(c0), uint32_t(a_row), 0u, a_dst_base + kStageBytesA * s, 8192u, smem_base + OFF_MAIN_FULL + 8u * s, 0, 0, 0, 0);
      }
#endif
      tma_load_2sm_mcast_3d(&params.tma_a, full_masked_base + 8u * s, a_mcast_mask, kCacheHintEvictNormal,
                            a_dst_base + kStageBytesA * s, c0, a_row, 0);                     // A: (64q, 128 tm + 64 y, 0), mask 0x5 << x
#if defined(CUTLASS_DEABSTRACTION_TRACE)   // [TRACE]
      if (TRACE_IN_FIRST_CLUSTER()) {
        TRACE_RECORD(K_TMA_LOAD, 128, uint32_t(c0), uint32_t(b_col), 0u, b_dst_base + kStageBytesB * s, 4096u, smem_base + OFF_MAIN_FULL + 8u * s, 0, 0, 0, 0);
      }
#endif
      tma_load_2sm_3d(&params.tma_b, full_masked_base + 8u * s, kCacheHintEvictNormal,
                      b_dst_base + kStageBytesB * s, c0, b_col, 0);                          // B: (64q, 128 tn + 64 x, 0)
    }
    --n;
    ++st.q;
  }
}
```

The two `#if defined(CUTLASS_DEABSTRACTION_TRACE)` blocks are the K4a probes of the diagnostics build; with the toggle off (the performance binary, note Part H.1) they compile to nothing, and `EXPLICIT_WAIT(addr, parity, site, tile, q)` is `mbar_wait(addr, parity)` (explicit.cu:237), so the `tile` parameter and the `uint32_t(st.q)` argument vanish too. What remains is a dozen statements. The parenthesised line numbers in the trailing comments (`:604`, `:607`, `:617`, `:619-622`) are lines of `sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp` and are exact in the working tree; `sm90_pipeline.hpp:531-539` is `PipelineTmaAsync::producer_acquire(stage, phase, token)` (verified: line 531 signature, 533 the token test, 534 the wait, 538 the `arrive_and_expect_tx`).

The parameters: `params` is the `__grid_constant__` parameter block (Chapter 5), needed only for `&params.tma_a` and `&params.tma_b`, the generic addresses of the two 128-byte `CUtensorMap`s in parameter space; `st` is the ring state; `n` is the number of k-tiles to issue in this call; `smem_base` is this CTA's 32-bit `shared::cta` base; the five invariants `a_dst_base`, `b_dst_base`, `full_masked_base`, `empty_base`, `a_mcast_mask` and the predicate `is_leader_lane` are computed once per role (Section 8.6.2); `a_row`/`b_col` are per tile (Section 8.6.3).

### 8.4.1 The pre-loop peek and the token (line 732)

```
  uint32_t tok = mbar_try_wait(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);            // producer_try_acquire before the loop (:604)
```

W7 (`mbar_try_wait`, explicit.cu:313-326) is one `mbarrier.try_wait.parity.shared::cta.b64` *without* a suspend-time hint followed by `selp.b32`: it returns 1 ("WaitDone": the phase of parity `prod_phase` has completed, the slot is free) or 0 ("WaitAgain"), and never loops. CUTLASS calls this `producer_try_acquire` (`sm90_pipeline.hpp:502-508`: when `skip_wait` is false it is exactly one `try_wait`). The token is computed *before* the loop so that the first iteration, like every later one, can decide with a single predicate whether it must block. Why peek at all instead of always calling the blocking form? Because the blocking form (W6) is a retry loop with a `NANOSLEEP`-backed `try_wait` that ptxas places out of line (note D.2: `TRYWAIT; @!P NANOSLEEP.SYNCS 0x989680; @!P SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64; @!P BRA`); the peek lets the common case skip the branch to that loop entirely, and it can be issued early (Section 8.4.5) so that its latency overlaps other work.

### 8.4.2 `#pragma unroll 1` (lines 733-734): why the k-tile loop stays rolled

```
  #pragma unroll 1                                                                          // CUTLASS_PRAGMA_NO_UNROLL (:607)
  while (n > 0) {
```

CUTLASS marks the same loop `CUTLASS_PRAGMA_NO_UNROLL` (`sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:607`). Three reasons, in decreasing importance:

1. **Nothing to gain.** Every iteration is dominated by two asynchronous TMA issues whose cost is paid by the TMA unit, not by this warp; the warp's own work is a dozen uniform-datapath instructions and it spends most of its life blocked on `empty[]` (Section 8.9). Unrolling cannot shorten a wait.
2. **Uniform-register pressure.** First the vocabulary, already used in the previous bullet and again in Section 8.9: uniform registers (`URn`, with `URZ` the uniform zero) are a per-warp scalar register file on the SM's *uniform datapath*, beside the per-lane vector registers (`Rn`); SASS instructions prefixed `U` (`UTMALDG`, `UIADD3`, `ULEA`, `UMOV`, `UPRMT`) execute once per warp on them, so a value that ptxas can prove warp-uniform — an address, a mask, a descriptor, a coordinate — costs no per-lane register and no per-lane work (Chapter 12 reads the SASS in detail). The baseline's tight resource is that uniform register file, not the vector file (note D.7, inferred from 44 uniform-to-vector spill/fill pairs in the CUTLASS kernel). An unrolled body would keep several stages' addresses and tokens live at once. Rolled, the loop needs one slot address, one token, one coordinate and the invariants.
3. **Code size and the perf contract.** The baseline's SASS has exactly two rolled producer loops of 8 and 120 iterations with one `UTMALDG.3D.MULTICAST.2CTA` and one `UTMALDG.3D.2CTA` each (note D.2, measured: "loop 1 counter runs -7..1 (8 iterations), loop 2 8..k_tiles (120); loop 2 body = 31 instructions"). The explicit kernel reproduces that shape (note G.3, measured: main loop 37 instructions, 33 on the fast path; prologue loop 37) — Section 12 of the note makes "same instruction-stream shape" part of the performance-equivalence contract.

### 8.4.3 The blocking wait only when the token says "not done" (line 735)

```
    if (!tok) { EXPLICIT_WAIT(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase, WAIT_MAINLOOP_EMPTY, tile, uint32_t(st.q)); }   // producer_acquire (sm90_pipeline.hpp:531-536)
```

W6 (`mbar_wait`, explicit.cu:296-311) is `LAB_WAIT: mbarrier.try_wait.parity.shared::cta.b64 P1, [addr], phase, ticks; @P1 bra DONE; bra LAB_WAIT;` with `ticks = 0x989680` = 10,000,000. The PTX ISA names the operand `timeHint` and fixes its unit: "The optional 32-bit unsigned integer operand timeHint specifies the time limit, in nanoseconds, that may be used for the time limit instead of the system-dependent limit" (PTX ISA 9.7.15.16.19, `mbarrier.test_wait` / `mbarrier.try_wait`), so the hint is 10 ms: CUTLASS's comment calls it an "Arbitrarily large timer value after which try-wait expires and re-tries" (`include/cutlass/arch/barrier.h:414`). The same ISA paragraph says the suspended thread "resumes execution when the specified phase completes OR before the phase completes following a system-dependent time limit": the hint *may* be used, so an early wake-up is legal, and the outer `bra LAB_WAIT` is what makes the wait correct rather than a fallback for a rare case. In practice a large hint means "sleep until released" with no busy polling. The `if (!tok)` is `if (barrier_token != BarrierStatus::WaitDone)` of `sm90_pipeline.hpp:533`.

### 8.4.4 The leader lane's `arrive.expect_tx` of 49152 bytes (line 736)

```
    if (is_leader_lane) { mbar_arrive_expect_tx_local(smem_base + OFF_MAIN_FULL + 8u * st.prod_idx, kMainloopTxBytes); }   // (:537-539), leader lane, 49152
```

W12 is `mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx.shared::cta.b64 _, [%1], %0;` (explicit.cu:381-390). The address is this CTA's **own** `full[s]`, unmasked, at `smem_base + 0 + 8 s` (`OFF_MAIN_FULL = 0`, explicit.cu:139). The byte count is

```
constexpr uint32_t kMainloopTxBytes  = 2 * (kStageBytesA + kStageBytesB);   // 49152: six 8192-byte boxes per stage credit the leader
```

(explicit.cu:180) with `kStageBytesA = 128 * 64 * 2 = 16384` and `kStageBytesB = 64 * 64 * 2 = 8192` (explicit.cu:116, 118). CUTLASS computes the same number as `TmaTransactionBytes` (`sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:238-240`): `size(AtomThrShapeMNK) = 2` times the per-CTA A stage (8192 fp16 = 16384 B) plus 2 times the per-CTA B stage (4096 fp16 = 8192 B). The derivation that matters is physical, not symbolic:

```
 49152 = 2 CTAs of the pair x (16384 B of A + 8192 B of B landing in each CTA)
       = 6 boxes x 8192 B
       = 4 A halves (one from each of the four CTAs of the cluster, Section 8.5) + 2 B halves (one from each CTA of the pair)
```

Every one of those six boxes names the pair leader's `full[s]` as its completion barrier (Section 8.4.6), so the leader's barrier is the single place where "the pair's whole 256 x 128 x 64 stage has landed" becomes observable — which is exactly what the leader's warp 0 needs before it may issue a `tcgen05.mma.cta_group::2` that reads both CTAs' smem (Chapter 9).

Three "why"s:

- **Why `arrive.expect_tx` as one instruction, and why count 1.** An mbarrier phase completes when the pending-arrival count reaches zero *and* the tx-count reaches zero — PTX ISA 9.7.15.16.8, "Phase Completion of the mbarrier object": "The count of the pending arrivals has reached zero. The tx-count has reached zero." (the LLVM NVPTX guide restates it as "An mbarrier object completes the current phase when: The count of the pending arrivals has reached zero AND The tx-count has reached zero"). `full[s]` is initialised with arrival count 1 (explicit.cu:182, `kMainFullCount = 1`; init by warp 0's elected lane — `if (warp_idx == 0) { if (elect_one_sync()) {` at explicit.cu:1122-1123, the loop at :1124-1128). The only arrival ever performed on it is this `arrive.expect_tx`, which atomically adds 49152 to the tx-count and then arrives. So the phase cannot complete before the expectation is registered, no matter in which order the six boxes land relative to this instruction — and they do land in arbitrary order: the peer's producer waited on its *own* `empty[s]`, released by the same two commits, and may run ahead of the leader's producer, so the peer's B box and A halves may credit the leader's barrier before the leader has even issued its `expect_tx`. What makes that order legal is a property of the counter itself: the tx-count is **signed**, with range `-(2^20 - 1) .. 2^20 - 1` (PTX ISA 9.7.15.16.3, "Contents of the mbarrier object", the same range for both mbarrier layouts), and the ISA's complete-tx operation simply says "tx-count is decremented by completeCount". A box that lands before the `expect_tx` drives the count to `-8192`, `-16384`, ... — a legal state, not an error — and the phase still cannot complete while the pending-arrival count is 1. The leader's one `arrive.expect_tx` is the single operation that both raises the tx-count by 49152 and drops the arrival count to 0; 49152 sits far inside the range (`2^20 - 1 = 1048575`). [the ordering argument is my analysis, resting on the ISA rules quoted; the kernel's value-equal runs would deadlock at `q = 0` if the rules were otherwise — the symptom in the first row of note E.7.2's failure-mode table.] One arrival, by one lane, is the minimum that keeps the completion gated; 32 arrivals (all lanes) would need count 32 and would buy nothing.
- **Why only the pair leader's lane.** `is_leader_lane` is `lane_pred != 0u && is_leader` at the call site (explicit.cu:1191): `lane_pred` is the result of the prologue's `elect_one_sync()` (explicit.cu:1103, one lane of each warp, fixed for the kernel's lifetime) and `is_leader` is `(rank & 1) == 0` (explicit.cu:1106). CUTLASS: `mainloop_pipeline_params.is_leader = lane_predicate && is_mma_leader_cta && is_participant.main_load` (`include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:465`). The peer never arrives on anything in the `full[]` array: not on its own barriers, not on the leader's.
- **Why the peer's `full[]` barriers exist but are never used.** Both CTAs run the same code with the same `SharedStorage` layout (the 2SM MMA requires identical smem layouts in the pair, note B.6), so the peer initialises its eight `full[]` barriers like everyone else (count 1) and then leaves them in phase 0 forever. Nothing waits on them (warp 0 of the peer skips the whole MMA section, Chapter 9) and nothing arrives on them (every TMA in the pair is redirected to the leader's by the peer-bit mask). They are 64 bytes of smem that keep the two CTAs' address maps identical. In SASS the arrive and the `MOV` that feeds its byte count are the loop's two lane-predicated *vector* instructions: `@!P0 MOV R5, 0xc000` and `@!P0 SYNCS.ARRIVE.TRANS64 RZ, [UR10], R5` (note G.3, measured). Mind the predicate sense: `P0` is the *complement* of `is_leader_lane`, so the `@!P0` guard executes both instructions in the one lane where `P0` is false — and in no lane at all in the peer. They cannot be uniform instructions because only one lane may execute them. A third instruction completes the picture: `VOTEU.ALL UP1, P0` votes the lane predicate into a uniform predicate (`UP1` true when every lane has `P0` set, i.e. when nobody arrives) and gates the arrive-address computation `@!UP1 ULEA UR10`, so the peer, where no lane arrives, skips the `ULEA` uniformly while the leader executes it (note G.3 for the instructions; the reading of the vote is mine).

### 8.4.5 Capture `s`, advance, peek the next stage — and the discarded peek (lines 737-739)

```
    uint32_t const s = st.prod_idx;                                                          // write_stage
    advance<kStages>(st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);
    tok = mbar_try_wait(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);                     // peek the next stage, unconditional (:617)
```

`s` is the slot this k-tile writes (`write_stage`, `sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:615`). The state advances *before* the TMA issue (`:616`), and the peek for the *next* slot is issued immediately (`:617`), unconditionally — CUTLASS passes no `skip_wait`. Two consequences:

- The peek's latency overlaps the TMA issue that follows; by the time the next iteration tests `tok`, the answer is usually in a register.
- The **last** iteration of every call peeks one slot past what the call will use, and that token is thrown away: `tok` is a local of `load_ktiles`, and the next call (or the next tile's first call) starts with its own pre-loop peek (line 732). Per tile that is `(8 + 1) + (120 + 1) = 130` peeks for 128 waits (note Section 7.5: "130 peeks per tile, 128 consumed"). A `try_wait` has no side effect on the barrier, so the two wasted peeks cost two `SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64.TRYWAIT` per tile and nothing else. The MMA warp, by contrast, predicates its peek off on the last k-tile (`consumer_try_wait(skip_wait)`, Chapter 9); the producer does not, and the explicit kernel mirrors each exactly.

### 8.4.6 One election, two TMA issues (lines 740-756)

```
    if (elect_one_sync()) {                                                                  // one election for the A+B pair (:619-622)
      int32_t const c0 = 64 * st.q;
```

W2 (`elect_one_sync`, explicit.cu:263-277) is `elect.sync`: exactly one lane of the converged warp gets the predicate. One election covers *both* TMA issues — the granularity CUTLASS uses (`sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:619-622`) and the granularity the note fixes as the contract (E.6.6: "one `elect_one_sync()` per TMA A+B pair"). It is a *fresh* election, not `is_leader_lane`: the arriving lane and the issuing lane may differ, and the issuing lane exists in every CTA (the peer issues its loads too), whereas `is_leader_lane` is false in the peer. In SASS no `ELECT` survives here: `UTMALDG` is a uniform-datapath instruction that issues once per warp whatever the number of active lanes, so ptxas folds the election away (note D.2, D.6 item 6) — the PTX form is what you write, the hardware form is what you get.

`c0 = 64 * st.q` is the innermost TMA coordinate: the k index of the first element of the box, in elements. A TMA coordinate tuple is `(innermost, outer, batch)` in **elements**, and each coordinate is a *signed* 32-bit integer — PTX ISA, `cp.async.bulk.tensor`: "The individual tensor coordinates in tensorCoords are of type .s32" — which is why `c0`, `a_row` and `b_col` are `int32_t`/`int` and W21/W22 bind them with the `"r"` constraint on `int32_t`. For the A and B maps the tuple is `(k, row, l)` (Chapter 5: the maps are encoded with mode order `(K, M, L)` / `(K, N, L)`, note Section 5.3). Elements of a box that fall outside the tensor are zero-filled: the maps are encoded with `CU_TENSOR_MAP_FLOAT_OOB_FILL_NONE` (note Section 5.3), the ISA's "Zero fill mode" ("Elements in the Bounding Box which fall outside of the tensor boundary are set to 0"). Nothing in this run is out of bounds (K = 128 x 64 exactly, note Section 10), but this is why a K that is not a multiple of 64 would still give the right D with this very loop: `k_tiles = (params.k + 63) >> 6` (explicit.cu:1112) rounds up, the last k-tile's tail columns of A and B read as zeros, and zeros contribute nothing to the accumulator [derived from source; the residue path is not exercised by the fixed run].

The A issue (W21, explicit.cu:449-460):

```
// W21 [TMA]  SM100_TMA_2SM_LOAD_MULTICAST_3D::copy (copy_sm100_tma.hpp:283-305); the barrier operand is already peer-bit-masked by the caller
__device__ __forceinline__ void tma_load_2sm_mcast_3d(void const* desc_ptr, uint32_t smem_int_mbar, uint16_t multicast_mask, uint64_t cache_hint,
                                                      uint32_t smem_int_ptr, int32_t crd0, int32_t crd1, int32_t crd2) {
  uint64_t gmem_int_desc = reinterpret_cast<uint64_t>(desc_ptr);
  asm volatile (
    "cp.async.bulk.tensor.3d.cta_group::2.shared::cluster.global.mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes.multicast::cluster.L2::cache_hint"
    " [%0], [%1, {%4, %5, %6}], [%2], %3, %7;"
    :
    : "r"(smem_int_ptr), "l"(gmem_int_desc), "r"(smem_int_mbar), "h"(multicast_mask),
      "r"(crd0), "r"(crd1), "r"(crd2), "l"(cache_hint)
    : "memory");
}
```

called as `tma_load_2sm_mcast_3d(&params.tma_a, full_masked_base + 8u * s, a_mcast_mask, kCacheHintEvictNormal, a_dst_base + kStageBytesA * s, c0, a_row, 0)`. Operand by operand:

| PTX operand | C++ argument | Value for this CTA | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `[%0]` destination (`shared::cluster`) | `a_dst_base + 16384 s` | `smem_base + 33792 + 16384 s + 8192 y` | This CTA's 64-row half goes to the upper (`y = 1`) or lower (`y = 0`) 8192 bytes of stage `s`. The multicast writes the *same CTA-relative offset* in every destination CTA (note B.6; Colfax: the operation "places the loaded data into the SMEMs of all CTAs specified by the bitmask"; gau-nernst: smem layouts "must be identical across cluster ranks" for exactly this reason), so both receivers get the half in the right place. The rank bits [24,26) in this address name the issuing CTA; the TMA uses the offset part for the other receiver. |
| `[%1, {%4,%5,%6}]` tensor map + coordinates | `&params.tma_a`, `(c0, a_row, 0)` | `(64 q, 128 tm + 64 y, 0)` | 64 k values (one 128-byte row of the box), 64 rows starting at this CTA's half, batch 0. The box is `(64, 64, 1)` fp16 = 8192 B (Chapter 5, note Section 5.3: the per-CTA A box is the 128-row tile *divided by the multicast count 2*, `copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp:1003-1008`). |
| `[%2]` mbarrier | `full_masked_base + 8 s` | `(smem_base & 0xFEFFFFFF) + 8 s` = the **pair leader's** `full[s]` | `.cta_group::2` lets the barrier operand name either CTA of the pair — PTX ISA, `cp.async.bulk.tensor`: "When .cta_group::2 is specified, the mbarrier object mbar can be in shared memory of either the same CTA as the shared memory destination dstMem or in its peer-CTA"; clearing address bit 24 selects the even rank (`Sm100MmaPeerBitMask = 0xFEFFFFFF`, `include/cute/arch/copy_sm100_tma.hpp:45`, applied at `:63/:89/:115` and, in `SM100_TMA_2SM_LOAD_MULTICAST_3D` (`:281-305`; its `copy` member is the `:283-305` of the W21 comment), at `:292`). With multicast, each destination CTA's signal goes to the barrier at that offset in *its* pair leader — ISA: "for each destination CTA specified in the ctaMask, the mbarrier signal is sent either to the destination CTA or its peer-CTA based on the %cluster_ctarank parity of the shared memory where the mbarrier object mbar resides" (note B.6; Colfax: "a CTA can find the address of its leader CTA's mbarrier by taking its own mbarrier address and setting the 24th bit to 0"). |
| `%3` ctaMask (`.b16`, `"h"`) | `a_mcast_mask` | `0x5 << x`: `0x5` (ranks 0, 2) for `x = 0`, `0xA` (ranks 1, 3) for `x = 1` | The two CTAs with the same `x` share `tm` (Section 8.5.4) and therefore need the same 128 A rows. Bit `i` of the mask = rank `i` receives the box. CUTLASS derives the mask with `create_tma_multicast_mask<2>` (`include/cute/atom/copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp:1500-1533`, reached through the projection overload at `:1536-1543`, which slices the `(v, m, n, l)` cluster layout at every mode but N); the explicit kernel writes the result (explicit.cu:772). |
| `%7` cache policy (`.b64`, `"l"`) | `kCacheHintEvictNormal` | `0x1000000000000000` | `TMA::CacheHintSm100::EVICT_NORMAL` (`include/cute/arch/copy_sm90_desc.hpp:194`), the default of CUTLASS's `with()` (`include/cute/atom/copy_traits_sm100_tma.hpp:182, 193`). The `.L2::cache_hint` qualifier is part of the copied string, so an operand must be supplied; EVICT_NORMAL is the neutral policy. In SASS it is the 64-bit `desc[UR32] = {0x0, 0x10000000}` (note G.3). |

The B issue (W22, explicit.cu:462-473) is the same instruction without `.multicast::cluster` and without the mask operand:

```
// W22 [TMA]  SM100_TMA_2SM_LOAD_3D::copy (copy_sm100_tma.hpp:104-128)
__device__ __forceinline__ void tma_load_2sm_3d(void const* desc_ptr, uint32_t smem_int_mbar, uint64_t cache_hint,
                                                uint32_t smem_int_ptr, int32_t crd0, int32_t crd1, int32_t crd2) {
  uint64_t gmem_int_desc = reinterpret_cast<uint64_t>(desc_ptr);
  asm volatile (
    "cp.async.bulk.tensor.3d.cta_group::2.shared::cluster.global.mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes.L2::cache_hint"
    " [%0], [%1, {%3, %4, %5}], [%2], %6;"
    :
    : "r"(smem_int_ptr), "l"(gmem_int_desc), "r"(smem_int_mbar),
      "r"(crd0), "r"(crd1), "r"(crd2), "l"(cache_hint)
    : "memory");
}
```

called as `tma_load_2sm_3d(&params.tma_b, full_masked_base + 8u * s, kCacheHintEvictNormal, b_dst_base + kStageBytesB * s, c0, b_col, 0)`: destination `smem_base + 164864 + 8192 s` (this CTA's whole 64 x 64 B stage, no `y` term), coordinates `(64 q, 128 tn + 64 x, 0)` (64 k values, this CTA's 64 of the 128 N columns of tile `tn`), the same pair-leader barrier, no multicast. B still carries `.cta_group::2`: that is what allows the barrier operand to be the leader's even though the data is purely local.

Why does the *peer* also issue loads at all, if only the leader computes? Because the 2SM MMA reads the peer's smem directly (Chapter 9, note B.6: "A rows [0,128) and B columns [0,64) of the 256x128 instruction come from the leader's smem and the remaining halves from the peer's smem at the same CTA-relative addresses"). The peer must therefore fill its own ring, and it must do so in lockstep slot-for-slot with the leader — which both producers do automatically because they wait on `empty[]` barriers released by the same commits.

Why the elected lane and not all 32 lanes? The PTX instruction is per-thread; 32 lanes would issue 32 copies of each box. (The epilogue's TMA *store* is deliberately issued by all 32 lanes of warp 4 because the baseline does so and ptxas turns it into one uniform `UTMASTG` anyway, Chapter 10 — a different history, same hardware outcome.)

### 8.4.7 `--n; ++st.q;` (lines 757-758)

`n` counts down the k-tiles of this call; `st.q` counts up the k index for the coordinate. In CUTLASS these are `--k_tile_count; ++k_tile_iter;` where the iterator is a plain integer for a rank-1 K mode (note B.3.1 step 11). Keeping both is what makes two calls per tile trivial: the second call starts at `st.q = 8` with `n = 120`.

---

## 8.5 Assembling a stage across the cluster

### 8.5.1 Who loads which rows and columns

Let the cluster's 256 x 256 tile start at CTA tile `(Tm, Tn)` with `Tm`, `Tn` even. Rank `r = x + 2y` works on CTA tile `(tm, tn) = (Tm + x, Tn + y)` (Section 8.5.4). Its loads:

| rank | `(x, y)` | tile `(tm, tn)` | A box rows (`a_row .. +64`) | A lands in (mask) | A offset in stage | B box columns (`b_col .. +64`) | B lands in |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | (0, 0) | `(Tm, Tn)` | `128 Tm + 0` | ranks 0, 2 (`0x5`) | `+0` | `128 Tn + 0` | rank 0 |
| 1 | (1, 0) | `(Tm+1, Tn)` | `128 (Tm+1) + 0` | ranks 1, 3 (`0xA`) | `+0` | `128 Tn + 64` | rank 1 |
| 2 | (0, 1) | `(Tm, Tn+1)` | `128 Tm + 64` | ranks 0, 2 (`0x5`) | `+8192` | `128 (Tn+1) + 0` | rank 2 |
| 3 | (1, 1) | `(Tm+1, Tn+1)` | `128 (Tm+1) + 64` | ranks 1, 3 (`0xA`) | `+8192` | `128 (Tn+1) + 64` | rank 3 |

### 8.5.2 The A-stage assembly diagram

```
 cluster tile (Tm, Tn): 256 rows of A (two tm) x 256 columns of B/D (two tn)

                 y = 0  (tn = Tn)                       y = 1  (tn = Tn + 1)
            +----------------------------+        +----------------------------+
  x = 0     | rank 0                     |        | rank 2                     |
  tm = Tm   | A stage s (16384 B):       |        | A stage s (16384 B):       |
            |  [+0    ] rows 128Tm+0..   | --+--> |  [+0    ] rows 128Tm+0..   |  <- loaded by rank 0, multicast 0x5: lands in ranks 0 and 2
            |  [+8192 ] rows 128Tm+64..  | <--+-- |  [+8192 ] rows 128Tm+64..  |  <- loaded by rank 2, multicast 0x5: lands in ranks 0 and 2
            | B stage s (8192 B):        |        | B stage s (8192 B):        |
            |  cols 128Tn + 0..63        |        |  cols 128(Tn+1) + 0..63    |  <- each CTA loads its own, no multicast
            +----------------------------+        +----------------------------+
  x = 1     | rank 1                     |        | rank 3                     |
  tm = Tm+1 |  [+0    ] rows 128(Tm+1)+0 | --+--> |  [+0    ] rows 128(Tm+1)+0 |  <- loaded by rank 1, multicast 0xA: lands in ranks 1 and 3
            |  [+8192 ] rows 128(Tm+1)+64| <--+-- |  [+8192 ] rows 128(Tm+1)+64|  <- loaded by rank 3, multicast 0xA: lands in ranks 1 and 3
            |  B cols 128Tn + 64..127    |        |  B cols 128(Tn+1)+64..127  |
            +----------------------------+        +----------------------------+
             \________ MMA pair {0,1} _______/     \________ MMA pair {2,3} _______/
              A: 256 rows [128Tm, 128Tm+256)        A: the same 256 rows
              B: 128 cols [128Tn, 128Tn+128)        B: 128 cols [128(Tn+1), +128)

 arrows = the direction of the multicast copy, from the issuing CTA into its sibling (same x, other y):
   the [+0] half is issued by the y = 0 CTA and flows left -> right into rank 2 / rank 3;
   the [+8192] half is issued by the y = 1 CTA and flows right -> left into rank 0 / rank 1
```

After the four A issues and the two B issues of a stage have landed, each CTA holds the *entire* 128 x 64 A stage of its own `tm` (its own half plus the half multicast by the sibling with the same `x`) and its own 64 x 64 B half. The pair leader's `tcgen05.mma.cta_group::2` then sees A as 256 rows (leader's 128 + peer's 128) and B as 128 columns (leader's 64 + peer's 64); each CTA's TMEM receives the 128 x 128 accumulator of its own `(tm, tn)` (Chapter 9).

[derived from source + measured] This is precisely what the K4a records of the first cluster show for `q = 0` (note D.1 D8; recomputed in Section 8.7.2).

### 8.5.3 The 49152-byte ledger of one leader barrier

Take the pair `{0, 1}` and its leader's `full[s]` (rank 0's, at `0x00000400 + 8 s`). Which boxes credit it? Every box whose destination CTA has rank 0 as pair leader, i.e. every box landing in rank 0 **or** rank 1:

| box | issued by | lands in | credits rank 0's `full[s]`? | credits rank 2's `full[s]`? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A rows `128Tm + 0..63` | rank 0 | ranks 0, 2 | yes (via rank 0) | yes (via rank 2) |
| A rows `128Tm + 64..127` | rank 2 | ranks 0, 2 | yes (via rank 0) | yes (via rank 2) |
| A rows `128(Tm+1) + 0..63` | rank 1 | ranks 1, 3 | yes (via rank 1, peer-bit) | yes (via rank 3, peer-bit) |
| A rows `128(Tm+1) + 64..127` | rank 3 | ranks 1, 3 | yes (via rank 1, peer-bit) | yes (via rank 3, peer-bit) |
| B cols `128Tn + 0..63` | rank 0 | rank 0 | yes | no |
| B cols `128Tn + 64..127` | rank 1 | rank 1 | yes (peer-bit) | no |
| B cols `128(Tn+1) + 0..63` | rank 2 | rank 2 | no | yes |
| B cols `128(Tn+1) + 64..127` | rank 3 | rank 3 | no | yes (peer-bit) |
| **total** | | | **6 x 8192 = 49152** | **6 x 8192 = 49152** |

Every A box credits *both* leaders because both pairs need all 256 A rows; each B box credits one leader because B is split, not shared. Per cluster and per k-tile the TMA unit moves 8 boxes = 65536 bytes from L2 and writes 4 x 24576 = 98304 bytes of shared memory (the A halves are written twice). Without 2SM and multicast, four independent 128 x 128 CTA tiles would read 4 x (16384 + 16384) = 131072 bytes per k-tile from L2 — twice as much [my analysis].

### 8.5.4 Why `tm % 2 == x`, hence `a_row = 128 tm + 64 y`

The comment on explicit.cu:777 says "tm % 2 == x for every tile this CTA receives (B.3.1 step 13)". Proof from the two mapping formulas:

- **Launch tile** (explicit.cu:1175-1176): `tm = 2 (blockIdx.y >> 1) + (blockIdx.x & 1)`, `tn = 2 (blockIdx.x >> 1) + (blockIdx.y & 1)`. The cluster is `(2, 2, 1)`, clusters tile the grid in `blockIdx` order, so `%cluster_ctaid.x = blockIdx.x & 1 = x` and `%cluster_ctaid.y = blockIdx.y & 1 = y` (explicit.cu:1173-1174 comments: `x == rank & 1`, `y == rank >> 1`; this is the `AlongN` transpose of `possibly_transpose_work_tile`, `include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm100_tile_scheduler.hpp:699-709`, where the grid's x indexes N and y indexes M). Hence `tm % 2 = blockIdx.x & 1 = x`.
- **CLC tile** (explicit.cu:692-693, Chapter 7): `tm = 2 (y0 >> 1) + (x0 & 1) + x`, `tn = 2 (x0 >> 1) + (y0 & 1) + y`, where `(x0, y0)` is the launch-grid id of the cancelled cluster's *first* CTA. A cluster's first CTA is cluster-aligned, so `x0` and `y0` are even (measured for all 991 cancelled responses, note D.3: "every valid first-CTA id is even"), the `& 1` terms vanish and `tm = y0 + x`, `tn = x0 + y`. Hence `tm % 2 = x` again.

So for any tile the CTA ever processes, `tm = Tm + x` with `Tm` even and `tn = Tn + y` with `Tn` even. The two CTAs with the same `x` (ranks `x` and `x + 2`, `y = 0` and `1`) have the same `tm` and need the same 128 A rows `[128 tm, 128 tm + 128)`; they split the work by `y`: rank `(x, y)` loads rows `[128 tm + 64 y, +64)` and multicasts them to both. That is `a_row = 128 tm + 64 y` (explicit.cu:777) with the destination `a_dst_base = smem_base + OFF_SMEM_A + 8192 y` (explicit.cu:768) so that the `y = 1` half lands in the upper 8192 bytes of the stage in both receivers. Symmetrically the two CTAs of a pair (same `y`) share `tn` and split B by `x`: `b_col = 128 tn + 64 x` (explicit.cu:778), destination `OFF_SMEM_B + 8192 s` (no `x` term: each CTA keeps only its own half, and the MMA reads the other half from the peer).

One substitution to know about, because it is the only place where the explicit kernel writes an expression *equivalent* to CUTLASS's rather than the same one. CUTLASS does not select the B half by `%cluster_ctaid.x`: its B coordinate is `128 tn + 64 V` with `V = cta_coord_v = rank % 2`, the CTA's position inside the MMA pair (note B.3.1 step 13: `tBgB = tBgB_nkl(_, tn, _, 0)`, coordinate `(0, 128*tn + 64V, 0)`; note B.4: `(64q, 128*tn + 64*(tm%2), 0)`), and its A coordinate is `256 (tm/2) + 128 V + 64 y`. The explicit kernel writes `64 x` and `128 tm + 64 y` because `V = rank % 2 = x = tm % 2` is an invariant of both tile mappings (proved above; `r = x + 2y` gives `rank % 2 = x`). The K4a records of Section 8.7.2 are the measured proof that the two forms produce the same coordinates.

Note Section 7.5 gives the same formulas with the cluster's launch coordinate: for the launch cluster at `(CX, CY)`, rank `r` loads A rows from `256 CY + 128 x + 64 y` and B columns from `256 CX + 128 y + 64 x`.

### 8.5.5 Why A is multicast across `y` and B is not multicast at all

Two CTAs that need the same operand tile can either each load it (two L2 reads) or have one load and multicast (one L2 read, two smem writes). Inside this cluster:

- The same **A** rows are needed by the two CTAs with equal `x` (different pairs). Nothing else connects those two CTAs, so the only way to share is TMA multicast. The 128-row tile is split into two 64-row halves so that both CTAs issue work and the L2 traffic is halved (note Section 5.3: `make_tma_atom_A_sm100` passes `num_multicast = 2` and the box is truncated from `(64, 128, 1)` to `(64, 64, 1)`).
- The same **B** columns are needed by the two CTAs of a pair. But the pair is already joined by the 2SM MMA, which reads both CTAs' smem; so B is *split*, each CTA loading its 64 columns, and no byte of B is written twice. Multicasting B across `x` would double the smem writes for nothing. (Colfax's cluster tutorial describes the general 1SM pattern — A multicast along cluster rows, B along cluster columns; with 2SM MMA the B sharing is absorbed by the instruction itself.) [derived from source; the design rationale is my analysis]

The trade-off that the design does *not* take: multicasting A across the pair (the two `tm` differ, so there is nothing to share) or using a 4-CTA multicast (no two CTAs beyond the `x`-pairs share A). The `(2,2,1)` cluster is exactly the shape in which every operand is loaded once per cluster.

---

## 8.6 producer_role (explicit.cu:762-807), line by line

```
__device__ __forceinline__ void producer_role(ExplicitGemmParams const& params, uint32_t smem_base, uint32_t x, uint32_t y,
                                              bool is_cta0, bool is_leader_lane, int k_tiles, int tm, int tn) {
  griddep_wait();                                                                              // wait_on_dependent_grids (kernel :620)
  ProducerState st;
  uint32_t thr_idx = 0, thr_phase = 1;      // CLC throttle producer (rank 0 only), 2 stages
  uint32_t clc_idx = 0, clc_phase = 0, clc_count = 0;   // CLC consumer, 2 stages
  uint32_t const a_dst_base       = smem_base + OFF_SMEM_A + kStageBytesAHalf * y;   // + 8192 * y: this CTA's 64-row half of the 128x64 A stage (B.4)
  uint32_t const b_dst_base       = smem_base + OFF_SMEM_B;
  uint32_t const full_masked_base = smem_base & kPeerBitMask;                    // (smem + 8 s) & 0xFEFFFFFF names the pair leader's full[s]
  uint32_t const empty_base       = smem_base + OFF_MAIN_EMPTY;
  uint16_t const a_mcast_mask     = static_cast<uint16_t>(0x5u << x);            // ranks x and x + 2 (create_tma_multicast_mask<2>)
  int tm_next = tm, tn_next = tn;
  uint32_t tile = 0;
  bool valid;
  do {
    int const a_row = 128 * tm + 64 * static_cast<int>(y);   // A rows of this CTA's half; tm % 2 == x for every tile this CTA receives (B.3.1 step 13)
    int const b_col = 128 * tn + 64 * static_cast<int>(x);   // B columns of this CTA's half
    st.q = 0;
#if defined(CUTLASS_DEABSTRACTION_TRACE)   // [TRACE]
    heartbeat(tile, HB_TILE_START);
#endif
    if (is_cta0) {                                                                             // throttle producer_acquire + producer_commit (kernel :632-636)
      EXPLICIT_WAIT(smem_base + OFF_THROTTLE_EMPTY + 8u * thr_idx, thr_phase, WAIT_THROTTLE_EMPTY, tile, 0u);   // blocking, no peek (PipelineAsync)
      mbar_arrive_local(smem_base + OFF_THROTTLE_FULL + 8u * thr_idx);                        // all 32 lanes (count 32)
      advance<kThrottleStages>(thr_idx, thr_phase);
    }
    int const k_tile_prologue = k_tiles < kPrologueKTiles ? k_tiles : kPrologueKTiles;        // min(Stages, k_tile_count) (kernel :629)
    load_ktiles(params, st, k_tile_prologue, smem_base, a_dst_base, b_dst_base, full_masked_base, empty_base, a_mcast_mask, is_leader_lane, a_row, b_col, tile);
    // (load_order_barrier.arrive() between the two load() calls is skipped: is_epi_load_needed is false for beta = 0)
    load_ktiles(params, st, k_tiles - k_tile_prologue, smem_base, a_dst_base, b_dst_base, full_masked_base, empty_base, a_mcast_mask, is_leader_lane, a_row, b_col, tile);
    __syncwarp();                                                                              // (kernel :664)
    valid = clc_consume<0u>(smem_base, x, y, clc_idx, clc_phase, clc_count, tm_next, tn_next, tile);   // consume response t AFTER this tile's loads (:666-671)
    tm = tm_next; tn = tn_next;                                                                // the fetched tile becomes current only here
    ++tile;
  } while (valid);
  // load_tail = producer_tail (sm90_pipeline.hpp:445-454): 8 blocking waits continuing the producer state (Section 7.10 tail 1)
  #pragma unroll
  for (int i = 0; i < kStages; ++i) {
    EXPLICIT_WAIT(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase, TAIL_MAINLOOP, tile, uint32_t(i));
#if defined(CUTLASS_DEABSTRACTION_TRACE)   // [TRACE]
    heartbeat(tile, HB_TAIL);
    trace_tail(TAIL_MAINLOOP, st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase, tile);
#endif
    advance<kStages>(st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);
  }
}
```

The "kernel :620", ":629", ":632-636", ":664", ":666-671" references are lines of `sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp` at CUTLASS commit cb424739 (the `copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp` line numbers in this chapter, by contrast, are those of the working tree, which is + 7 lines from cb424739 in the encoder region and + 32 from :1078 on; Chapter 1 lists the four shifted headers); the working tree on this branch carries 28 extra lines of trace probes after line 614 (`git diff cb424739 HEAD` on that file: hunks at 614, 729, 870), so the same statements are at :648 (`wait_on_dependent_grids`), :657 (`k_tile_prologue`), :661-662 (throttle), :668 and :682 (the two `load` calls), :678 (`load_order_barrier.arrive`), :692 (`__syncwarp`), :693 (`fetch_next_work`), :705 (`load_tail`) today. The call site is explicit.cu:1191, inside the `if (warp_idx == 2) {` ... `}` of :1190-1192: `producer_role(params, smem_base, x, y, is_cta0, lane_pred != 0u && is_leader, k_tiles, tm, tn);`.

### 8.6.1 `griddep_wait()`: what PDL does here (line 764)

W35 is `griddepcontrol.wait;` (explicit.cu:599). CUTLASS emits it because the build defines `CUTLASS_ENABLE_GDC_FOR_SM100=1` (note B.3.1 step 10, measured D14), and places it in the producer warp *before any global-memory access* (`sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:646-648`: "Ensure that the prefetched kernel does not touch unflushed global memory prior to this instruction"). Under Programmatic Dependent Launch a dependent grid may start before its predecessor has finished; `griddepcontrol.wait` blocks until the prerequisite grids have completed and flushed their memory (CUDA Programming Guide, PDL section: `cudaGridDependencySynchronize()` "will block until all primary kernels the secondary kernel is dependent on have completed and flushed results to global memory"). This launch carries **no** PDL attribute — `run()` sets exactly one launch attribute, the cluster dimension (explicit.cu, Section 11; note Section 5.4: `launch_with_pdl == false`), so there are no prerequisite grids and the instruction completes at once [derived: PTX semantics + the launch configuration]. It still costs one `ACQBULK` in SASS (note G.3: `ACQBULK` 2 = warp 2 and rank-0 warp 1). Why keep it? Semantics preservation: the CUTLASS kernel executes it, and if a user later launched this kernel with PDL after a producer of A/B, the wait is what makes the TMA loads read the finished data. The matching `griddepcontrol.launch_dependents` is issued by warp 0 after its last tile (Chapter 9). The baseline executes it in **three** warps: warp 2 (`sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:648`), the scheduler (`:716`) and the epilogue-*load* warp 3 (`:844`, under `else if (is_participant.epi_load)`, placed before its TMA loads of C for `beta != 0`). The explicit kernel keeps the first two (explicit.cu:764, :821) and drops the third together with the whole warp-3 path (`beta = 0`; warp 3 exits after barrier initialisation, Chapter 11) — hence `ACQBULK` 2 in the explicit SASS against 3 in the baseline (note G.3 vs D.2; the note's `check_sass.py` dry run on the baseline dumps lists "`griddepcontrol.wait` 3 (the epilogue-load warp's)" among the rows where the baseline legitimately differs from the explicit contract). Warps 4-7 wait in neither kernel: their only global-memory traffic is the TMA store of D, whose data derives from A and B loaded after warp 2's (or warp 3's) wait [my analysis].

### 8.6.2 The invariants (lines 765-775)

| local | value | why it is hoisted / why this value |
|---|---|---|
| `st` | `{0, 1, 0}` | Section 8.3. |
| `thr_idx, thr_phase` | `{0, 1}` | Throttle *producer* state (2 slots): producers start at phase 1, so CTA 0's first two tiles pass the throttle wait without blocking (the two slots are initially free). |
| `clc_idx, clc_phase, clc_count` | `{0, 0, 0}` | CLC *consumer* state (2 slots): consumers start at phase 0 and block until the first response lands (Chapter 7). |
| `a_dst_base` | `smem_base + 33792 + 8192 y` | `OFF_SMEM_A = 33792` (explicit.cu:154) plus this CTA's half offset; `kStageBytesAHalf = 8192` (explicit.cu:117, "equal to kStageBytesB by coincidence of the tile shape" — the half of a 128 x 64 fp16 tile happens to equal a 64 x 64 fp16 tile). |
| `b_dst_base` | `smem_base + 164864` | `OFF_SMEM_B` (explicit.cu:155). |
| `full_masked_base` | `smem_base & 0xFEFFFFFF` | `kPeerBitMask` (explicit.cu:187). Because `OFF_MAIN_FULL = 0`, `full[s]` is `smem_base + 8 s`, and masking the base once is the same as masking every `(smem_base + 8 s)`: the mask touches only bit 24 and `8 s <= 56` cannot carry into it from a base whose low 24 bits are `0x400`. Measured values: `0x00000400` for ranks 0 and 1, `0x02000400` for ranks 2 and 3 (note D.1 D5: `base & 0xFEFFFFFF` is the even partner's base). nvcc folds known-zero low bits into the constant: `0xFEFFFFF8` in the CUTLASS kernel (three alignment bits of an 8-byte barrier, note D.6 item 2) and `0xFEFFFFF0` here (`and.b32 ..., -16777232`, since the base itself is masked; note G.3) — identical results for these addresses. The source comment at explicit.cu:187 ("nvcc folds it to 0xFEFFFFF8") is true of the epilogue's accumulator-release site only (`0x44c0`, note G.3): do not look for `0xFEFFFFF8` in the producer's SASS, where the fold is `0xFEFFFFF0` on the hoisted base. |
| `empty_base` | `smem_base + 64` | `OFF_MAIN_EMPTY` (explicit.cu:140). |
| `a_mcast_mask` | `0x5 << x` (16-bit) | Section 8.4.6. The `"h"` constraint needs a `uint16_t`. |
| `tm_next, tn_next, tile, valid` | `tm, tn, 0, -` | The CLC consume writes the *next* tile into `tm_next/tn_next`; the current tile stays in `tm/tn` until the end of the loop body (Section 8.6.7). `tile` is the tile counter, used only by the trace. |

Hoisting these is not an optimisation nvcc needed help with — it is the discipline of note D.7 ("the explicit kernel should keep loop-invariant operands few (descriptor bases, masks, barrier bases) and let ptxas keep them uniform"), restated as a rule in note E.6.6. In the measured SASS four of them are nevertheless re-materialised per k-tile, in five instructions (the B tensor-map address, the mask insert `UPRMT ..., 0x5410`, the z coordinate, `0xc000`); they are the largest part of the *net* +6 instructions over the baseline's loop — eight explicit-only instructions minus two baseline-only ones, note G.3; the full ledger is in Section 8.9 — and, as Section 8.9 argues, cost nothing.

### 8.6.3 Per-tile setup (lines 777-779)

`a_row` and `b_col` are recomputed from the current `(tm, tn)` (Section 8.5.4) and `st.q` is reset to 0 — but `st.prod_idx/prod_phase` are not touched: the ring continues.

### 8.6.4 The throttle producer on CTA 0 (lines 783-787)

```
    if (is_cta0) {                                                                             // throttle producer_acquire + producer_commit (kernel :632-636)
      EXPLICIT_WAIT(smem_base + OFF_THROTTLE_EMPTY + 8u * thr_idx, thr_phase, WAIT_THROTTLE_EMPTY, tile, 0u);   // blocking, no peek (PipelineAsync)
      mbar_arrive_local(smem_base + OFF_THROTTLE_FULL + 8u * thr_idx);                        // all 32 lanes (count 32)
      advance<kThrottleStages>(thr_idx, thr_phase);
    }
```

The throttle is a CTA-local, two-slot `PipelineAsync` between rank 0's warp 2 (producer) and rank 0's warp 1, the scheduler (consumer, Chapter 7). Barriers: `throttle_full[2]` at `OFF_THROTTLE_FULL = 304`, `throttle_empty[2]` at `OFF_THROTTLE_EMPTY = 320`, both count 32 (explicit.cu:148-149, 185; initialised by warp 3, explicit.cu:1155-1162). The producer side is `PipelineAsync::producer_acquire(state)` with the default `WaitAgain` token — a blocking wait with no peek (`sm90_pipeline.hpp:1110` and `:1185-1189`) — followed by `producer_commit` = one `mbarrier.arrive.shared::cta.b64` per thread (`:1193-1196`), hence "all 32 lanes (count 32)" and W9 at explicit.cu:345-354. The scheduler consumes `throttle_full[i]` and releases `throttle_empty[i]` with 32 remote arrives to CTA 0 (itself) — the generic `PipelineAsync` release form, which is why `kThrottleCount = 32` on both sides.

What it is for: the scheduler issues CLC query `t` (which fetches tile `t + 1`) only after it has consumed `throttle_full` for tile `t`, i.e. only after rank 0's warp 2 has *started issuing the loads of tile `t`*. Without the throttle, the scheduler could run two queries ahead (two CLC slots) and the cluster would hoard tiles it cannot start yet — bad load balance at the end of the grid, where idle clusters would find the queue empty while busy clusters sit on prefetched tiles. With it, a cluster holds at most one tile beyond the one its producer is loading (note D.7: "keep at most one query outstanding per cluster beyond the tile being loaded"; measured D.3: "never more than one query was outstanding per cluster (0 violations in 1024 queries)"). Why warp 2 and not warp 0 as the throttle producer? Warp 2 is the earliest warp to commit to a tile (it runs up to 8 stages ahead of the MMA), so tying the query to warp 2's progress issues it as early as the "one ahead" rule allows, giving the response (median latency 1.4 us, note D.3) the most time to arrive before anyone needs it [my analysis]. Why blocking without a peek? The wait almost always passes immediately and it happens once per tile; the peek machinery would be noise. *How* far ahead the release is follows from the ring having two slots: warp 2's wait on `throttle_empty[t % 2]` at tile `t` is for the phase the scheduler completed when it consumed `throttle_full[t % 2]` for tile `t - 2` and released the slot right away (explicit.cu:836-838: wait `throttle_full`, 32 remote arrives on `throttle_empty`, advance). The release warp 2 depends on is therefore about two tile periods old — about 2 x 27.8 us = 56 us in the Release run (0.889354 ms over 32 tiles), 2 x 31.9 us in the trace build (note D.3's per-tile time) [the `t - 2` relation is derived from the code; the per-tile times are measured; the product is my inference]. The first two tiles pass on the inverted start phase (two slots, both initially free). Note D.3's 28.8-37.7 us (median 30.8 us) is a *different* number: the scheduler's gap from consuming response `n` to issuing query `n + 1`, i.e. how long the scheduler sits in its `throttle_full` wait per tile — the measurement that shows the scheduler, not warp 2, is the one who waits. Why two slots rather than one? With one slot, warp 2 at tile `t + 1` would block until the scheduler had woken up and consumed tile `t`'s arrive; with two, warp 2 can arrive for tile `t + 1` before the scheduler has consumed tile `t`'s, so the producer is never gated on the scheduler's wake-up latency while the scheduler is still held to one query ahead [my analysis; the 2 is the baseline's stage count, note Section 7.2, `kThrottleStages = 2` at explicit.cu:110].

### 8.6.5 `k_tile_prologue` and the two `load_ktiles` calls (lines 788-791)

```
    int const k_tile_prologue = k_tiles < kPrologueKTiles ? k_tiles : kPrologueKTiles;        // min(Stages, k_tile_count) (kernel :629)
```

`kPrologueKTiles = kStages = 8` (explicit.cu:107, 115); `k_tiles = (params.k + 63) >> 6 = 128` (explicit.cu:1112). The first call issues `min(8, k_tiles)` k-tiles — one full pass over the ring, which never blocks on a fresh ring (Section 8.3) — and the second issues the remaining `k_tiles - 8 = 120`. Why two calls? In CUTLASS, between them sits

```
        if (do_load_order_arrive) {
          load_order_barrier.arrive();
          do_load_order_arrive = false;
        }
```

(`sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:677-680`): when `beta != 0` the epilogue's C-load warp (warp 3) may start its TMA loads of C only after the mainloop producer has filled the ring once, so that the mainloop gets a head start on the TMA unit and L2. For `beta = 0` the arrive is skipped (`is_epi_load_needed` is false; the explicit kernel does not even initialise the load-order barrier, explicit.cu:141-143, "reserved, not initialised") — but the two `load` calls remain in the baseline, and each becomes its own rolled loop in SASS: "two rolled loops (8 and 120 iterations)" (note D.2, measured). The explicit kernel keeps two calls for the same reason it keeps `#pragma unroll 1`: the instruction-stream shape is part of the contract, and the semantics are identical either way (the state lives in `st`, and the second call re-peeks before its loop, Section 8.4.5). For `k_tiles <= 8` the second call runs zero iterations (its pre-loop peek still executes once, harmlessly); for `k_tiles == 0` both do.

### 8.6.6 `__syncwarp()` (line 792)

W37, `bar.warp.sync -1`. CUTLASS: "Sync warp to prevent non-participating threads entering next wave early" (`sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:691-692`). In the PTX model only the elected lane executed the TMA issues; the other 31 lanes could run ahead into the CLC consume, and the consume contains a warp-collective wait. The `__syncwarp` reconverges the warp first. In SASS it produces no instruction (note D.2: "warp 2's per-tile `__syncwarp()` produced no instruction") because ptxas folded the election into uniform instructions, leaving no divergence to repair. You write it for the PTX contract.

### 8.6.7 `clc_consume` after the loads (lines 793-795)

```
    valid = clc_consume<0u>(smem_base, x, y, clc_idx, clc_phase, clc_count, tm_next, tn_next, tile);   // consume response t AFTER this tile's loads (:666-671)
    tm = tm_next; tn = tn_next;                                                                // the fetched tile becomes current only here
    ++tile;
```

`clc_consume` (Chapter 7) waits on this CTA's `clc_full[idx]`, decodes the 16-byte response, fences, arrives remotely on CTA 0's `clc_empty[idx]` (this warp's 32 arrivals are part of the 800), advances the 2-slot state and, if the response is a cancelled cluster, writes the next tile into `tm_next/tn_next`. The template argument `0u` means "no trace record" (explicit.cu:238-239).

**Why after the loads, when warps 0 and 4-7 consume before their work?** Each warp consumes exactly one response per loop iteration, so over the kernel every warp consumes the same sequence; only the position inside the body differs. Response `t` (giving tile `t + 1`) is requested when rank 0's warp 2 passes the throttle at the start of tile `t`, and arrives about 1.4 us later (median, note D.3). If warp 2 consumed it *before* issuing tile `t`'s loads, it would stall ~1.4 us at every tile start with the ring draining — a bubble the MMA warp would feel eight k-tiles later. Consuming *after* the 128 k-tiles of loads (which take roughly 28 us, because the producer is paced by the ring) finds the response long since landed; the consume is free. Warps 0 and 4-7 consume *before* computing or storing tile `t`: when they reach that point, the producer has already been in tile `t` for a while (it runs ahead), so the response is usually there too, and consuming first lets them hold the next tile's coordinates for the whole body (Chapter 9, Chapter 10). The baseline's comment and code order (`fetch_next_work` at `:693` after the loads; `:730` before `mma()`; `:854` before `store()`) is preserved exactly. [derived from source; the latency reasoning is my analysis supported by note D.3's measurements]

**Why `tm = tm_next` only here.** `a_row`/`b_col` for the current tile were computed from `tm/tn` at the top of the body and must not change under the loads; the fetched tile becomes current at the end of the body, as in CUTLASS (`work_tile_info = next_work_tile_info` at `:698`). The loop ends when a response is *not cancelled* (`valid == false`): no unstarted clusters remain anywhere in the grid (Chapter 7).

### 8.6.8 The tail: eight blocking waits, parity 1 (lines 797-806)

```
  #pragma unroll
  for (int i = 0; i < kStages; ++i) {
    EXPLICIT_WAIT(empty_base + 8u * st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase, TAIL_MAINLOOP, tile, uint32_t(i));
    ...
    advance<kStages>(st.prod_idx, st.prod_phase);
  }
```

This is `load_tail` -> `PipelineTmaAsync::producer_tail` (`sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:633-640`, `sm90_pipeline.hpp:448-454`: `for (count < Stages) { empty_barrier_ptr_[state.index()].wait(state.phase()); ++state; }`). It **continues the producer state** where the loop left it; it does not apply one parity to all eight barriers (note Section 7.2 warns against that).

**Proof that every tail step waits parity 1 for any tile count.** Let `n_tiles` be the number of tiles this CTA processed (31 or 32 in the fixed run, note D.3; it is spelled out because the lecture's `T` is the TMEM base of Chapters 9-10). After `n_tiles` tiles the producer has made `N = 128 n_tiles` steps. Step `i` of the tail (`i = 0..7`) is step `N + i` of the state and waits on `empty[(N + i) % 8]` with parity `1 ^ (((N + i) / 8) & 1)`. Since `128 n_tiles % 8 = 0`, `(N + i) % 8 = i` and `(N + i) / 8 = 16 n_tiles` for `i < 8`; `16 n_tiles` is even for every `n_tiles`, so the parity is `1 ^ 0 = 1` and the slot is `i`: the tail waits on `empty[0..7]` in order, each with parity 1. [derived] Measured: 1518 `K_TAIL` records in the traced run, 8 `TAIL_MAINLOOP` per CTA with `idx 0..7` and parity 1 in every one of the 132 CTAs ("every mainloop tail step waited parity 1, `k_tail_mainloop_parity` PASS", note G.1).

**What parity 1 means at that moment.** Stage `i` was used `16 n_tiles` times (16 times per tile: 128 k-tiles over 8 slots), each use completing one phase of `empty[i]` (two commit arrivals). The barrier is in phase `16 n_tiles`; the most recently completed phase is `16 n_tiles - 1`, odd, parity 1. `try_wait.parity(1)` therefore returns true exactly when the *last* use of stage `i` has been released by both pair leaders — the commits for k-tiles `120 + i` of the final tile. For a hypothetical shape where some stage is never used, its barrier is still in phase 0 and parity 1 passes immediately — CUTLASS's own comment: "if the stage was never used then would just be acquired since the phase was still inverted" (`sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp:634-639`). Hard-coding parity 1 would be correct for this shape and wrong in general (e.g. 72 k-tiles per tile gives `9 n_tiles` passes, odd after an odd number of tiles, so the tail would then have to wait parity 0); continuing the state is correct always.

**Why the tail exists.** There is no cluster-wide barrier at kernel exit (note Section 7.10). Two things would go wrong without it:

1. The last `tcgen05.commit` of each pair leader multicasts arrivals (mask `0xF`) into *this* CTA's `empty[]`; if this CTA had exited, a remote `mbarrier.arrive` would target freed shared memory (undefined; note B.6, `mbarrier.*.shared::cluster` rule).
2. Worse, the 2SM MMA of this CTA's pair leader reads this CTA's smem stages directly, and the leader of the *other* pair reads nothing of ours but our producer wrote into its sibling's A slots. Waiting on `empty[0..7]` — released only after *both* leaders' MMAs have finished reading every stage — guarantees that nobody is still reading shared memory this CTA is about to give up. The peer's warp 0 has no tail of its own on this ring (it never consumed it), so warp 2's eight waits are the only thing keeping a peer alive until its leader's last MMA has retired. [derived from source; note Section 7.10 "guard (1)"]

**Why `#pragma unroll` here (explicit.cu:798), when both k-tile loops are `#pragma unroll 1`.** The tail mirrors `producer_tail`'s `for (count < Stages)` over a compile-time bound, which nvcc unrolls in the baseline as well ("`producer_tail` = 8 unrolled waits", note D.2), and note E.6.6 makes the shape part of the contract ("tails as unrolled `for` over compile-time `Stages`"). It runs once per kernel, so its code size is irrelevant, and unrolling removes the counter and the back-branch: what remains is eight waits, each followed by `advance`'s state update. In SASS that is eight waits with the `UIADD3 +1; UISETP.NE.U32 ..., 8; USEL; LOP3 ... 0x3c` sequence between them, and the warp's `EXIT` follows the last (baseline: tail `0x2660-0x2a60`, the last wait with an inline retry loop, `EXIT` at `0x2a90`, note D.2; explicit kernel: warp 2's `EXIT` at `0x1980`, note G.3 — the note records no start address for the explicit tail).

## 8.8 What the TMA unit does on write: SWIZZLE_128B

The producer passes *linear* destination addresses (`a_dst_base + 16384 s`, `b_dst_base + 8192 s`) and never computes a swizzled offset, yet the bytes do not land linearly: both tensor maps are encoded with `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B` (Chapter 5; note Section 5.3, measured D3), and the UMMA descriptors declare `layout_type = 2` = SWIZZLE_128B (`include/cute/arch/mma_sm100_desc.hpp:114`; explicit.cu:171 `kSmemDescHi`). Writer and reader agree on the same permutation, so the kernel can be oblivious to it (explicit.cu:203: "applied by the TMA unit on write and by the UMMA unit on read (SWIZZLE_128B); the kernel never computes it").

### 8.8.1 `Swizzle<3,4,3>`

CuTe's `Swizzle<BBits, MBase, SShift>` (`include/cute/swizzle.hpp:54-68`) XORs `BBits` bits of an offset, located `MBase` bits up (`zzz_msk`), with the `BBits` bits `SShift` further up (`yyy_msk`): `apply(o) = o ^ ((o & yyy_msk) >> SShift)`. For `<3,4,3>`: `zzz_msk = 0b111 << 4 = 0x70` (bits [4,7)), `yyy_msk = 0b111 << 7 = 0x380` (bits [7,10)); explicit.cu:204 asserts exactly `yyy_msk == 0x380` and `num_shft == 3`. On a byte address:

```
 physical = pre ^ (((pre >> 7) & 7) << 4)
```

Bits [4,7) are the index of the 16-byte chunk inside a 128-byte row; bits [7,10) are the row index modulo 8. So: **inside each 1024-byte atom (8 rows x 128 B), chunk `c` of row `r` is stored at chunk position `c ^ (r % 8)`.** The CUDA Programming Guide states the same rule for the 128B mode as `smem[y][((y + offset) % 8) ^ x]` with `x` the 16-byte unit, `y` the row, and `offset = (smem_ptr / 128) % 8` (its Table 24, "Swizzle Pattern Pointer Offset Formula and Index Relation"): `offset` is the row-within-atom position of the buffer's *start address*, added to the row index because the hardware swizzles on absolute address bits, not on offsets from the buffer's start. For a 1024-byte-aligned base `offset = 0` and the Guide's formula collapses to the `chunk ^ (row % 8)` above; every base in this kernel is such a base (Section 8.8.3). The pattern repeats after 8 rows = 1024 bytes.

### 8.8.2 One stage, drawn

Plain (pre-swizzle) byte offset of A element `(m, k)` in stage `s`: `16384 s + 128 m + 2 k` (K-major: 64 fp16 = 128 B per row `m`; the CuTe layout at explicit.cu:124-125, `((_128,_16),_1,_4,(_1,_8)) : ((_64,_1),_0,_16,(_0,_8192))` in elements, says the same: row stride 64 elements, k-block stride 16 elements = 32 B, stage stride 8192 elements). For B element `(n, k)`: `8192 s + 128 n + 2 k`. Since `2 k < 128`, bits [7,10) of the plain offset are `m % 8`, so the physical byte is `16384 s + 128 m + ((2 k) ^ ((m % 8) << 4))`; the 16-byte chunk `k >> 3` of row `m` sits at chunk `(k >> 3) ^ (m % 8)`.

```
 one 1024-byte atom = rows m..m+7 of a stage (128 B each); entries = logical chunk (8 fp16 = 16 B) stored at that physical position

 physical chunk ->    0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7        <- the 8 x 16 B = 128 B of one row
 row m%8 = 0        [ 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 ]      k 0-7, 8-15, ..., 56-63 in order
 row m%8 = 1        [ 1 | 0 | 3 | 2 | 5 | 4 | 7 | 6 ]
 row m%8 = 2        [ 2 | 3 | 0 | 1 | 6 | 7 | 4 | 5 ]
 row m%8 = 3        [ 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 ]
 row m%8 = 4        [ 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 ]
 row m%8 = 5        [ 5 | 4 | 7 | 6 | 1 | 0 | 3 | 2 ]
 row m%8 = 6        [ 6 | 7 | 4 | 5 | 2 | 3 | 0 | 1 ]
 row m%8 = 7        [ 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 ]

 A stage s = 16 such atoms (rows 0-7, 8-15, ..., 120-127), 16384 B, at smem_base + 0x8400 + 0x4000 s
   the y = 0 half (rows 0-63) = atoms 0-7 at +0, the y = 1 half (rows 64-127) = atoms 8-15 at +8192: each multicast box is 8 whole atoms
 B stage s = 8 atoms (rows 0-63), 8192 B, at smem_base + 0x28400 + 0x2000 s
 k-block kb of a k-tile = logical chunks 2 kb and 2 kb + 1 of every row (32 B = 16 fp16): the UMMA descriptor's start address advances by 32 B per kb
```

Why this pattern? Shared memory is banked 32 x 4 B = 128 B wide, so one row covers all banks and a *column* of chunks (the same `k` range in 8 consecutive rows) would hit the same four banks eight times. XORing the chunk index with the row index spreads those eight accesses over all eight chunk positions, i.e. all 32 banks — the CUDA Programming Guide's "each matrix element is from a different bank for both the rows and columns, and so without any bank conflicts". The UMMA reads core matrices of 8 rows x 16 B at a time; with the swizzle it reads them conflict-free [derived; the UMMA's internal access pattern is the hardware's business].

### 8.8.3 Why 1024-byte alignment, and why the kernel never computes the swizzle

Both units apply the XOR to **absolute shared-memory address bits**, not to offsets within a box or a tile. The row index they use is address bits [7,10). For that to equal `m % 8`, the stage base must contribute zeros in bits [7,10): `base % 1024 == 0`. The kernel guarantees it three times over: `OFF_SMEM_A = 33792 = 33 x 1024` and `OFF_SMEM_B = 164864 = 161 x 1024` (explicit.cu:162, `static_assert(OFF_SMEM_A % 1024 == 0 && OFF_SMEM_B % 1024 == 0, "SW128 stage bases need 1 KiB alignment (Section 7.5)")`), the stage strides 16384 and 8192 and the half offset 8192 are multiples of 1024, and the dynamic base's low 24 bits are `0x400 = 1 x 1024` (measured, note D.1 D5; the kernel declares no static `__shared__`, explicit.cu Section 10 banner, so the dynamic buffer starts right after the 1 KiB of system-reserved shared memory). Which of these is hardware-mandatory and which is a design choice? The CUDA Programming Guide's hard requirement for a swizzled TMA destination is **128-byte** alignment (its Table 25, "Shared memory alignment", 128 bytes for every swizzle mode); 1024 is only a recommendation ("For simplicity shared memory should be aligned according to the number of bytes after which the swizzle pattern repeats"). A destination that is 128-byte but not 1024-byte aligned is legal for the TMA: the pattern is simply shifted by `offset = (addr / 128) % 8` rows (Section 8.8.1). What makes 1024 a *hard* requirement for this kernel is the reader. The UMMA descriptor carries a 3-bit `base_offset` field (`mma_sm100_desc.hpp:112-113`) precisely for a start address whose bits [7,10) are not zero, and CUTLASS leaves it at 0 (`constexpr uint8_t base_offset = 0; desc.base_offset_ = base_offset;`, `mma_sm100_desc.hpp:757-758`); the explicit kernel's `kSmemDescHi = 0x40004040` (explicit.cu:171) has zeros in those bits too (Chapter 9). With `base_offset = 0` the UMMA assumes the stage has `offset = 0`, so the TMA side must be handed a base with `offset = 0` as well — 1024-byte aligned. The dependency chain is: the TMA requires 128 B; the UMMA with `base_offset = 0` requires 1024 B; the kernel chooses `base_offset = 0`, as CUTLASS does, and therefore pays 1024-byte alignment on `OFF_SMEM_A`, `OFF_SMEM_B`, the stage strides and the dynamic base [derived from source; the Guide's two statements are quoted from its async-copies page].

Because the permutation is a function of the address, the UMMA can start a k-block *inside* an atom: the descriptor's start address `+ 32 kb` has bits [4,7) = `2 kb`, which the hardware XORs with the row bits of each row it fetches, landing on the right chunks. This is why the producer can write 64-wide k-tiles with one box while the MMA consumes them in four 16-wide k-blocks without anybody shuffling data. The kernel's only swizzle arithmetic is the epilogue's `Swizzle<2,5,2>` on *its own* `st.shared` stores (Chapter 10), where the writer is software; here both writer and reader are hardware.

### 8.8.4 Why the k-tile is 64

For `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B` the inner box dimension may be at most 128 bytes: the CUDA Programming Guide's Table 25 gives "Shared box's inner dimension <= 128 bytes" for the 128B mode, and the layer that enforces it is the driver — the CUDA Driver API reference for `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled` states "CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B* require the bounding box inner dimension to be <= 128" and lists `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE` among its returns. CuTe performs *no* check of this rule: its encoder (`copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp:1011-1020`) asserts only the generic box limits, `1 <= boxDim[i] <= 256` (the Driver API's "must be non-zero and less than or equal to 256"), and `:1022-1031` the `1..8` element-stride limits. 128 bytes of fp16 is `128 / 2 = 64` elements, so one TMA box covers at most 64 k values — and the UMMA's SW128 K-major canonical layout is exactly 8 rows x 64 fp16. The name to follow is `UMMA::Layout_K_SW128_Atom<ElementType>`, which `sm100_smem_selector` (`include/cutlass/gemm/collective/builders/sm100_common.inl:82`, the branch at `:116-117`) picks because `BLK_K = 64` is a multiple of the atom's K extent; that name is an alias (`using cute::GMMA::Layout_K_SW128_Atom;`, `include/cute/atom/mma_traits_sm100.hpp:71`) of the definition in namespace `SM90::GMMA` (`include/cute/atom/mma_traits_sm90_gmma.hpp:84` in bits — `ComposedLayout<Swizzle<3,4,3>, smem_ptr_flag, Layout<Shape<_8,_1024>,Stride<_1024,_1>>>` — and `:104` typed), so a reader searching for the UMMA name must hop through the alias. A k-tile of 64 is therefore the widest unit the swizzled TMA box, the swizzled UMMA descriptor and one `mbarrier` phase can all agree on; four `tcgen05.mma` of K = 16 consume it (Chapter 3 for the design arithmetic, Chapter 9 for the descriptor increments). The 64 x 64 boxes respect the 256-element limit with room to spare.

---

## 8.9 The footprint of warp 2, and why its loop length does not matter

What the loop keeps live (per k-tile): the slot index and phase (`st.prod_idx`, `st.prod_phase`), the token, `n`, `st.q`, and the invariants of Section 8.6.2 — two destination bases, the masked barrier base, the empty base, the mask, the cache hint (64-bit), two tensor-map addresses (constant-bank addresses, `&params.tma_a/b`), `a_row`, `b_col`, and the two predicates (`is_leader_lane`, the fresh election). Nothing is indexed at run time, nothing lives in local memory: the whole kernel reports `REG 26, LOCAL 0, STACK 0` (note G.3, measured). For a learner who wants to reproduce that count: note G.3 records the highest vector register as `R23` against the baseline's `R65` ("hence `REG` 26 vs 68") and attributes the baseline's surplus to state the explicit kernel does not carry — the zero-filled C fragment, the epilogue-load state and its 44 spill/fill pairs. [my analysis: the 26 is set by the epilogue warps, which hold 16 `tcgen05.ld` results plus `alpha`, `beta` and store addresses live at once — the largest per-thread working set in the kernel — not by this warp, whose state is almost entirely uniform.]

Measured shapes (note G.3 vs D.2): the explicit kernel's main producer loop is 37 SASS instructions (33 on the fast path, i.e. when the peek succeeded) against the baseline's 31 (28); the 8-iteration prologue loop 37 against 32. The +6 is a *net* figure (note G.3): eight explicit-only in-loop instructions minus two baseline-only ones. The eight: five re-materialisations of four loop invariants (`@!P0 MOV R5, 0xc000`; the B tensor-map parameter address `UIADD3 UR30, ..., UR22, 0x80` + `UIADD3.X UR31`; the multicast-mask insert `UPRMT UR34, URZ, 0x5410, UR25`; the z coordinate `UMOV UR20, URZ`), the warp vote `VOTEU.ALL UP1, P0`, the predicated arrive-address `@!UP1 ULEA UR10`, and `ULEA UR17, UR28, UR35, 0x3` for the masked `full[s]` address. The two the baseline has and the explicit kernel does not: an unconditional arrive-address `ULEA` (replaced by the predicated one) and a per-k-tile `ULOP3 ..., 0xfefffff8` peer-bit mask (replaced by the `ULEA` on a base that nvcc had already masked with `& 0xfefffff0`, Section 8.6.2). All but the lane-predicated `MOV R5` and the `VOTEU.ALL` are uniform-datapath instructions (Section 8.4.2 for the term). The issue order wait -> `expect_tx` -> peek -> TMA A -> TMA B is identical.

Why none of this is on the critical path [my analysis from measured numbers]: the fixed run takes 0.889354 ms for 32 tiles x 128 k-tiles on the busiest clusters, about 217 ns = 427 cycles at 1965 MHz per k-tile, and that time is set by the tensor core executing four 256 x 128 x 16 MMAs per k-tile and by the TMA/L2 delivering 24576 bytes per CTA per k-tile. The producer's 33-37 instructions issue in a few dozen cycles and then the warp *blocks on `empty[]`*: it is allowed to run eight k-tiles (about 1.7 us) ahead of the MMA, and after the first ring pass it is always waiting for a slot, not working. The ring depth (8 stages, chosen as the largest number fitting the 227 KiB opt-in smem after the epilogue's 33792 bytes and the barrier carve-out — `floor((232448 - 192 - 33792) / 24592) = 8`, note Section 6.1) is what hides the TMA round trip, not the loop length. The same holds for the MMA warp's 47-instruction loop (Chapter 9) relative to the hundreds of cycles of tensor-core work per k-tile. A producer loop would start to matter only if it approached the per-k-tile budget, roughly an order of magnitude away.

---

## 8.10 Carrying this to other kernels

- **One barrier per shared resource, owned by the consumer that needs the whole resource.** The pair leader's `full[s]` sums the pair's bytes because the leader's MMA is the single consumer of the pair's stage. When you design a multi-CTA operand, ask "who issues the instruction that needs all of it?" and route every `complete_tx` there; then `expect_tx = sum of everything that lands in the consumer's domain`, and the arrival count is the number of distinct *arrivers*, not of boxes.
- **Multicast where CTAs share data and nothing else joins them; split where an instruction already spans the CTAs.** A across `y` (shared `tm`, no other link), B across the pair (joined by `cta_group::2`).
- **Peek-then-wait, and continue the state across tiles and into the tail.** The parity bookkeeping is the entire correctness of a ring; compute it from a running counter, never from the tile shape.
- **Keep producers oblivious to layout transforms that hardware applies symmetrically.** The TMA writes swizzled, the UMMA reads swizzled; your job is alignment (1024 B) and box shape (inner dim <= 128 B), not XORs.
- **Order the slow consume after the fast issue.** Any per-tile handshake whose latency is comparable to a pipeline refill (the CLC response here) belongs after the work that keeps the pipeline busy.
- **Tails are not optional in cluster kernels.** Every barrier that a remote CTA can still arrive on, and every smem region a remote instruction can still read, needs a wait before `EXIT`.

Sources opened for this chapter (besides the local tree and the note): the CUDA C++ Programming Guide, "Asynchronous Data Copies" (Table 24: the TMA swizzle rule `smem[y][((y+offset)%8)^x]` with `offset = (smem_ptr/128)%8`; Table 25: the 128-byte shared-memory alignment requirement and the <= 128 B inner box; the "for simplicity" 1024-byte alignment recommendation), https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/04-special-topics/async-copies.html; the CUDA C++ Programming Guide, "Programmatic Dependent Launch and Synchronization", https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/04-special-topics/programmatic-dependent-launch.html; the PTX ISA itself (CUDA 13.x "Parallel Thread Execution ISA", read as a local text dump): `cp.async.bulk.tensor` (`.cta_group::2` barrier placement, the multicast signal rule, `.s32` coordinates), `mbarrier` 9.7.15.16.3/.8/.19 (tx-count range, phase completion, `timeHint`), `griddepcontrol`, and the tensor-map "Zero fill mode"; the LLVM NVPTX user guide as a secondary statement of the same mbarrier rules ("An mbarrier object completes the current phase when: The count of the pending arrivals has reached zero AND The tx-count has reached zero"; "The %timelimit operand (an unsigned integer) specifies the limit in nanoseconds"), https://llvm.org/docs/NVPTXUsage.html; the CUDA Driver API reference, `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled` (the <= 128-byte inner box for `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B*`, the <= 256 `boxDim` limit, `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE`), https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-driver-api/group__CUDA__TENSOR__MEMORY.html; Colfax Research, "CUTLASS Tutorial: GEMM with Thread Block Clusters on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs" (leader CTA = even rank, the bit-24 peer barrier address, `tma_transaction_bytes` scaled by the pair), https://research.colfax-intl.com/cutlass-tutorial-gemm-with-thread-block-clusters-on-nvidia-blackwell-gpus/; gau-nernst, "tcgen05 for dummies" (2-CTA MMA: both CTAs' TMA report to CTA 0's barrier; identical smem layouts required for multicast), https://gau-nernst.github.io/tcgen05/. PTX ISA section numbers for `cp.async.bulk.tensor .cta_group::2` and `mbarrier` are as listed in note B.6; every ISA sentence quoted above was checked against the ISA text itself.
